passport.market: EUR/USD (first choice), GBP/USD or USD/JPY on raw-spread pricing; one pair per session. M5 for the setup, M1 for optional entry refinement, H1 for bias.

M5 20 EMA above the 50 EMA, both sloping, with a fresh M5 high in the last hour. Price pulls back into the 20–50 EMA value band, ideally at a pre-marked micro level, without closing beyond the 50 EMA.
passport.trigger: An M5 candle that closes back in the trend direction from the value band — bullish engulfing, rejection pin bar or a close through the prior candle's high (mirror for shorts). Enter on a stop order 0.2 pips beyond the trigger candle; cancel if unfilled within two candles.

lessons.title: What Scalping Is — and Who Should Not Do It
lessons.summary: Define scalping strictly, list what the format demands, and decide honestly whether you are the narrow profile it suits before you risk a penny on it.
lessons.html:
Scalping has the best marketing in retail trading. Quick trades, small stops, money made before the coffee goes cold. The reality is less photogenic: scalping is the most expensive trading format per pip of edge, the most mentally fatiguing, and the least forgiving of sloppiness. It can be done well. Most people who try it do it badly, and the reasons are structural rather than personal.

This course teaches one complete scalping method — a four-step plan on the 5-minute chart with optional refinement on the 1-minute — and it teaches the arithmetic and the operating discipline that decide whether that method has any chance of working for you. We will be honest throughout, including in this first lesson, where the honest answer for many readers is "not yet, and possibly not ever". That is a perfectly good outcome. It costs a few evenings rather than an account.

A definition worth being strict about

Scalping is taking many small, short-duration trades on low timeframes — usually the 1-minute and 5-minute charts — held for minutes rather than hours, and judged inside the session they were opened. The scalper is not trying to ride a trend from start to finish. The aim is to capture a small, repeatable slice of a move that the market's short-term behaviour makes likely: a pullback ending inside a trend, a level holding after a test, a session open pushing in the direction the bigger picture already favours.

In this course a scalp has four fixed properties. It has a defined trigger, an observable candle event you could point at on a screen. It has a stop measured in single-digit pips on the major pairs — five to eight pips on EUR/USD in our plan. It has a target fixed in advance as a multiple of that stop, which we will call R. And it has a holding time short enough that the trade is usually resolved within half an hour.

That rules out a lot of what people call scalping. Two trades a day held for three hours is day trading. Closing a swing trade early because it frightened you is not scalping either; it is nerves with a fast exit. The distinction matters because the numbers change completely once targets shrink to single digits.

The core ratio: error and cost as a fraction of target

Here is the single idea that drives the whole course. Every trade pays a toll — spread, commission and slippage — and every trader makes small execution errors. Those tolls and errors are roughly fixed in pips. Your target is not.

A swing trader aiming for 80 pips who enters a pip late has given away just over 1% of the target. A scalper aiming for 7.5 pips who enters a pip late has given away 13%. Add a typical all-in toll of around 1 pip and the scalper is surrendering more than a quarter of every winner before the market has done anything at all. Lesson 2 does this arithmetic properly. For now, hold on to the shape of it: small targets do not reduce cost, they concentrate it.

KEY POINT

In scalping, cost and error are measured as a fraction of your target. Shrink the target and the same one-pip mistake becomes a much bigger share of your edge.

What the format actually demands

It is worth listing the demands bluntly, because each one is a legitimate reason not to scalp.

Time, in unbroken blocks. You cannot scalp around a job by glancing at a phone. The plan in this course trades one of two windows — the London open or the London–New York overlap — and needs your full attention for around two hours. Miss a trigger by thirty seconds and it has gone.

Cheap, fast execution. You need raw-spread pricing, low commission, a platform that does not freeze when the market gets busy, and fills you have measured rather than read about. Costs that are trivial for a swing trader decide whether a scalper can win at all.

One rehearsed play. Fast decisions only stay accurate when they are binary: is this my setup, yes or no? A trader with five setups on a 1-minute chart is answering an essay question every candle. This course gives you one setup, and asks you to drill it until recognising it takes seconds.

Emotional durability. A normal session might hold four to six trades. Losses cluster. You can follow every rule and still take three losers in a row before ten o'clock, purely from variance. If that sequence makes you change the rules, the format will take you apart.

Hard limits, set in advance. Because the trade cycle is fast, drawdowns are fast. A bad hour of scalping can do what a bad month of swing trading does. Daily loss limits and trade caps are structural parts of the method, not optional extras, and Module 4 treats them that way.

Who should not scalp

Here is the editorial position of this course, stated early so nobody can say it was buried: most traders should not scalp, and almost nobody should start their trading life with it.

The reasons are not about intelligence.

Costs. As Lesson 2 shows, scalping pays the highest toll per pip of edge of any format. You need a genuinely strong edge just to break even, whereas a trader on the 4-hour chart can survive with a modest one.

Feedback. Scalping produces so many trades that bad habits are reinforced dozens of times a week before you notice them. A swing trader who chases entries does it twice a month. A scalper who chases does it twice an hour.

Physiology. Sustained rapid decision-making under financial pressure is tiring, and fatigue degrades exactly the discipline the format depends on. The rule-follower at 08:15 is often a rule-bender by 10:00.

Life. If your free time is in the evening, you are looking at the Asian session on European pairs: thin, slow and relatively expensive. That is not a scalping market for EUR/USD or GBP/USD, and no amount of enthusiasm changes it.

So who is it for? A narrow profile: someone with proven discipline on higher timeframes, who can follow written rules under pressure, has two free hours at a consistent time that overlaps London or New York, has access to genuinely low-cost execution, and finds repetition calming rather than boring. If that is not you today, the honest move is to keep trading slower formats and come back to this course when it is.

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating scalping as an easier route into trading because the stops are small. Small stops mean small losses per trade, but a fast cycle and a fixed toll mean losses accumulate quickly. Scalping is the advanced course, not the beginner's shortcut.

What "mastery" means in this course

Mastery here is not predicting price to the pip. Nobody does that. It means four precise things:

  1. Precise knowledge of your costs — your all-in round-trip toll, measured, written on a card.
  2. A precisely defined setup — the four-step 5-minute plan, with every condition stated so that two honest people watching the same chart would agree whether it triggered.
  3. Precise execution — orders chosen in advance, stops attached at entry, size pre-set, the emergency exit rehearsed.
  4. Precise limits on your behaviour — a daily loss limit, a trade cap, a consecutive-loss breaker and a session that ends by the clock.

The course is built in that order. Module 1 handles costs, sessions and pairs. Module 2 builds the four-step 5-minute plan. Module 3 covers 1-minute execution, candle triggers and trade management. Module 4 builds the operating system around you: limits, psychology, journaling, and a capstone playbook with complete worked trades — including losers and a session where the correct number of trades was zero.

Going deeper

For experienced traders, three points that are often misunderstood.

Scalping is a variance problem disguised as a speed problem. Because each trade risks a small amount, people assume scalping is low risk. Per trade, it is. Per session, it is not. Six trades at 0.5% risk can lose 3% in a morning; the same trader on a 4-hour chart might take three weeks to do that. What matters is how fast your daily distribution of outcomes is sampled, and scalping samples it very quickly. That is why the daily limit, not the per-trade stop, is the scalper's most important risk control.

Your edge has to survive a toll that other formats barely notice. If a strategy has a modest positive expectancy before costs — say a hypothetical +0.15R per trade — a 4-hour trader paying a toll of 0.02R keeps almost all of it. A scalper paying 0.2R per trade turns the same raw edge into a loss. Many people's 1-minute "edges" are real; they are just smaller than the toll.

Sample sizes arrive fast, which is the one genuine advantage. A swing trader needs two years to collect 200 trades. A scalper on a simulator can collect them in a couple of months. That makes scalping unusually testable. Use that advantage: the method in this course is designed to be logged, measured and judged on a few hundred simulated trades before any money is involved.

THE RULES
  • Scalp only if you can commit two uninterrupted hours inside the London or London–New York window
  • Trade one written setup, on one pair, in one session — no improvisation
  • Measure your all-in round-trip cost before you take a single live scalp
  • Every scalp has a stop attached at entry and a fixed target set in R
  • Simulate first: at least 200 logged trades before any live risk

Summary

  • Scalping is many small, short trades on M1 and M5, with single-digit-pip stops and targets fixed in R, judged inside the session.
  • The defining ratio is cost and error as a fraction of target; small targets concentrate cost rather than reducing it.
  • The format demands unbroken time, cheap execution, one rehearsed setup, emotional durability and hard limits — all at once.
  • Most traders should not scalp; concluding that from honest testing is a success, not a failure.
  • This course gives one complete method — the 4-step 5-minute plan — and the arithmetic and discipline to judge it.

quiz.q: Which of these best fits this course's strict definition of a scalp?
options: Two trades a day, each held for three hours
A swing trade closed early because it moved against you
A defined trigger, a 5–8 pip stop on EUR/USD, a target fixed in R, resolved within the session
Any trade taken on the 1-minute chart
quiz.why: A scalp has a defined trigger, a small fixed stop, a target fixed in R and a short holding time. Timeframe alone does not make a trade a scalp, and long holds are day trading.

quiz.q: A scalper targeting 7.5 pips enters one pip late. Roughly what share of the target has that error cost?
options: About 1%
About 5%
About 13%
About 50%
quiz.why: 1 ÷ 7.5 ≈ 13%. The same pip on an 80-pip swing target would be just over 1% — which is why execution errors matter so much more to scalpers.

quiz.q: In the 'one session, many decisions' chart, the second long is stopped out after a valid entry. What is the correct verdict?
options: The entry was wrong because it lost
The stop should have been moved lower
It was a correct decision with a losing outcome
The trader should double size on the next trade
quiz.why: A valid setup that loses is still a correct decision. Judging decisions by single outcomes is how scalpers start rewriting rules mid-session.

quiz.q: Why is the daily loss limit described as the scalper's most important risk control?
options: Because per-trade stops are unreliable on M1
Because scalping samples the daily outcome distribution very quickly, so losses can stack within hours
Because brokers require it
Because it guarantees a profitable month
quiz.why: Each scalp risks little, but many trades in a short window can compound losses fast. The daily limit caps the session, not just the trade.

quiz.q: A trader can only trade between 21:00 and 23:00 UK and wants to scalp EUR/USD. What does this lesson suggest?
options: Scalp anyway with wider stops
That window is thin and relatively expensive for EUR/USD; trade a slower format instead
Use the 1-minute chart to compensate
Trade five pairs to find more setups
quiz.why: Late-evening UK hours are thin for European pairs. The format needs the busy, cheap hours, so a slower format suits that schedule better.

lessons.title: The Cost Maths — Spread, Commission, Slippage and Your Break-Even Win Rate
lessons.summary: Calculate your all-in round-trip cost, express it in R, and work out the break-even win rate it forces on any stop and target before you take a scalp.
lessons.html:
Every trade you take pays a toll at the gate: the spread, any commission, and whatever slippage happens between the price you wanted and the price you got. For a trader holding positions for days, the toll is a rounding error. For a scalper it is the most important number in the business — more important than the entry pattern, the indicator settings or the pair.

This lesson does the arithmetic in the open. By the end you will have one number written on a card — your all-in round-trip cost in pips — and you will know exactly what that number does to the win rate your scalping needs just to stand still. If the answer is uncomfortable, better to find out here than six months into a live account.

All numbers in this lesson are illustrative. They sit in a realistic range for a raw-spread retail account on a major pair, but your broker, pair and hours will differ, and part of the job is measuring your own.

The three parts of the toll

Spread. The gap between the bid and the ask. You buy at the ask and sell at the bid, so every round trip — in and out — pays the spread once. On a raw-spread account during busy London hours, EUR/USD might typically show 0.1 to 0.3 pips. On a "no commission" standard account it might show 0.8 to 1.2 pips, because the broker's charge is folded into the spread.

Commission. Raw-spread accounts charge a fee per lot instead. A common structure is about $7 per standard lot per round turn. On EUR/USD, where one pip on one standard lot is worth $10, that is 0.7 pips. Notice the conversion, because it changes by pair — more on that in Going deeper.

Slippage. The difference between the price you clicked and the price you were filled. It is not printed on any rate card, and it is largest at exactly the moments scalpers like to trade: session opens, fast breaks and stop runs. You only learn your slippage by logging intended price against filled price on every trade.

Add them and you get the all-in round-trip cost. For our illustrative EUR/USD scalper trading the London window on a raw account: 0.2 spread + 0.7 commission + 0.1 average slippage = 1.0 pip. That is the number we will use throughout the course. Write yours down when you have measured it.

Same toll, different targets

Here is why that 1.0 pip matters so much more to a scalper than to anyone else.

The swing trader pays 1 pip against a 60-pip target: 1.7%. The scalper pays 1 pip against a 7.5-pip target: 13%. Against the 5-pip stop it is 20% — a fifth of a full loss, paid on every trade, win or lose. The market charges everyone the same entry fee; the scalper simply buys a much smaller ride with it.

KEY POINT

Express your toll in R. A 1-pip cost on a 5-pip stop is 0.2R — paid on every single trade, before the market does anything.

What costs do to your break-even win rate

Now the uncomfortable part. Let S be your stop in pips, T your target in pips and C your all-in cost in pips. After costs, a winner nets T − C and a loser costs S + C. The win rate at which you exactly break even is:

Break-even win rate = (S + C) ÷ (S + T)

Or, in R terms, with R = T ÷ S as your reward-to-risk and c = C ÷ S as your cost in R:

Break-even win rate = (1 + c) ÷ (1 + R)

Three worked examples, all illustrative:

  • The classic "5 and 5" scalp with a 1.3-pip toll: (5 + 1.3) ÷ (5 + 5) = 63%. Without costs it would be 50%. The toll alone moved the bar thirteen points.
  • This course's plan: 5-pip stop, 1.5R target (7.5 pips), 1.0-pip toll: (5 + 1) ÷ (5 + 7.5) = 48%. Without costs, 40%.
  • A tight 1-minute scalp: 3-pip stop, 4.5-pip target, same 1.0-pip toll: (3 + 1) ÷ (3 + 4.5) = 53%. Shrinking the stop made the trade harder to win with, not easier.

That third example deserves a moment. The beginner's instinct — "use a tighter stop and take quicker profits, it's safer" — is exactly backwards for a scalper. A tighter stop makes the fixed toll a larger fraction of R, which pushes the required win rate up.

Here is the full table. Read across for your target in R; read down for your cost in R.

Cost in R (c) Target 1R Target 1.5R Target 2R
0 (no costs) 50% 40% 33%
0.1 55% 44% 37%
0.2 60% 48% 40%
0.3 65% 52% 43%
0.5 75% 60% 50%

Two patterns stand out. First, every 0.1R of cost adds roughly four to five percentage points to the win rate you need at 1R or 1.5R. Second, a cost of 0.5R — which is what a 2-pip toll on a 4-pip stop gives you — makes a 1R scalp need 75% winners. Very few repeatable strategies live there.

The 5x rule

To keep the arithmetic workable, this course uses one simple constraint: your stop must be at least five times your all-in round-trip cost. That caps your cost at 0.2R or below. With a 1.0-pip toll, the minimum stop is 5 pips; with a 1.4-pip toll on GBP/USD, it is 7 pips.

If the chart's logical stop is closer than that, you cannot shrink the cost, so you have two honest options. Either place the stop at the minimum distance — further from price than the structure strictly requires, with position size reduced so the money at risk is unchanged — and accept that the 1.5R target is now further away too. Or, if the market does not have room for that larger target, skip the trade. What you may not do is keep the tight stop and pretend the toll is someone else's problem. A setup that only works with a 3-pip stop on a 1-pip toll is not a setup you can afford.

COMMON MISTAKE

Choosing a tight stop because it allows a bigger position size. Size is not the problem; the toll is. The same 0.5% account risk on a 3-pip stop pays proportionally far more in costs than on a 6-pip stop.

Slippage: the cost nobody quotes you

Spread and commission are known before you trade. Slippage is not, and it concentrates exactly where scalping opportunities appear.

Three practical consequences follow.

  1. Measure it. Log intended price and filled price for every trade, entry and exit. Your real cost base is unknowable without it.
  2. Prefer orders that cap it where your setup allows. A limit order caps entry slippage at zero, at the price of sometimes not being filled. Lesson 7 covers that trade-off.
  3. Treat news as a cost event, not an opportunity. Around scheduled high-impact releases, spreads can widen to many times normal for seconds or minutes. A 4-pip spread on a 7.5-pip target is not a trade; it is a donation.

The cost audit

Before you scalp a single unit of real money, do this homework. It takes two weeks of a few minutes a day.

  1. Open a demo or small live account with the broker you intend to use.
  2. At the times you intend to trade, record the actual spread on your chosen pair every 15 minutes for ten trading days.
  3. Convert the commission into pips at your intended size and pair.
  4. Run 20 practice orders and log intended versus filled price.
  5. Write one number on a card: your all-in round-trip cost, using a bad-but-normal case (the 80th or 90th percentile of your spread readings, not the average).

Then hold that card against the 5x rule. If your cost is 1.0 pip, your minimum stop is 5 pips and your minimum 1.5R target is 7.5 pips. If the setups you see on your pair rarely need stops that wide, or the moves rarely travel that far in your window, the format does not fit your costs. Change the broker, change the pair — or, honestly, change the format.

Going deeper

Commission converts differently by pair. $7 per lot round turn is 0.7 pips on EUR/USD and GBP/USD, where a pip is worth $10 per lot. On USD/JPY at 150.00, a pip on one lot is worth about $6.67, so the same $7 is about 1.05 pips. On some crosses it is higher still. Always convert commission into pips for the specific pair before you compare brokers or pairs.

Averages flatter you. A spread that averages 0.2 pips but sits at 0.6 pips for the first five minutes of the London open is a 0.6-pip spread for most of your entries, because that is when your entries happen. Measure cost at the moment you trade, not across the day.

Expectancy is fragile to small cost changes. Take a hypothetical strategy that wins 52% of the time at a 1.5R target. With a toll of 0.2R, each winner nets 1.3R and each loser costs 1.2R: expectancy = 0.52 × 1.3 − 0.48 × 1.2 = +0.10R per trade. Double the toll to 0.4R (a standard account with a 2-pip all-in cost) and the same trading gives 0.52 × 1.1 − 0.48 × 1.4 = −0.10R per trade. The pattern, the discipline and the trader are identical; the sign flips on the account type. These numbers are invented to show the mechanism, not a claim about any strategy.

Cost per hour matters too. Two scalpers with the same per-trade cost and edge differ if one takes six trades a session and the other takes fifteen. If the extra nine trades are lower quality, they pay the full toll for less edge. Lesson 10 turns this into a trade cap.

THE RULES
  • Know your all-in round-trip cost (spread + commission + measured slippage) in pips before trading
  • Minimum stop = 5x round-trip cost, so cost never exceeds 0.2R
  • If the structural stop is closer than the minimum, widen to the minimum (sizing down) or skip — never trade the tight stop
  • Log intended versus filled price on every entry and exit
  • Be flat before scheduled high-impact news and wait until spreads normalise afterwards

Summary

  • Your toll is spread + commission + slippage, measured in pips per round trip; our illustrative EUR/USD figure is 1.0 pip.
  • The same toll is a rounding error on a swing trade and a fifth of the risk on a 5-pip scalp.
  • Break-even win rate = (1 + c) ÷ (1 + R): costs push it up, and tighter stops push it up further.
  • The 5x rule keeps cost at or below 0.2R; a tighter structural stop is widened to the minimum or the trade is skipped.
  • Slippage concentrates at opens, breaks and news — log it, and treat news windows as cost events.

quiz.q: With a 6-pip stop, a 9-pip target and a 1.2-pip all-in cost, what is the break-even win rate?
A trader tightens their stop from 5 to 3 pips and keeps a 1.5R target and a 1.0-pip cost. What happens to the break-even win rate?
options: It falls, because losses are smaller
It stays the same, because R is unchanged
It rises, because cost becomes a larger fraction of R
It cannot be calculated
quiz.why: Cost in R rises from 0.2 to 0.33, so break-even rises from 48% to about 53%. Tighter stops concentrate the fixed toll.

quiz.q: Your all-in cost on GBP/USD is 1.4 pips. Under the 5x rule, what is your minimum stop?
options: 5 pips
7 pips
10 pips
14 pips
quiz.why: 5 × 1.4 = 7 pips, which keeps cost at 0.2R.

quiz.q: Which part of the toll can you only discover by logging your own fills?
options: Spread
Commission
Slippage
Pip value
quiz.why: Slippage — the gap between intended and filled price — is not published anywhere and varies with market speed.

quiz.q: In the slippage chart, a buy-stop fills 1.2 pips above the order price on a 5-pip-stop trade. How much extra cost is that in R?
options: It is not a cost because the trade may still win
quiz.why: 1.2 ÷ 5 = 0.24R. Slippage is a cost whether the trade wins or loses.

quiz.q: A hypothetical strategy has positive expectancy on a raw-spread account but negative expectancy on a standard account with the same trades. What is the most likely reason?
options: The standard account has worse charts
The higher all-in toll in R flipped the sign of a small edge
Standard accounts fill winners slower
This cannot happen if the strategy is good
quiz.why: A small edge can be entirely consumed by an extra 0.1–0.2R of cost per trade. The trading is identical; only the toll changed.

lessons.html:
Lesson 2 established that the toll is fixed and the target is small. This lesson is about getting the most movement for that toll. A scalper pays roughly the same cost per trade whether the market is busy or asleep, so the question becomes: when, and on what, does that toll buy the most opportunity?

The answer is narrower than most traders expect. One major pair, perhaps two. One session window, defined to the minute. And a calendar of hours you never trade, however tempting the chart looks. That narrowness is not a limitation. Every variable you remove is a decision you no longer have to get right thirty times a morning.

The pulse of the forex day

The forex market trades around the clock, but it does not pay attention around the clock. On the European pairs, the day has a pulse with three distinct phases.

The Asian session (roughly midnight to 08:00 UK in winter, an hour earlier in summer) is typically quiet for EUR/USD and GBP/USD. The desks that dominate those pairs are mostly asleep. Ranges are narrow, movement is choppy, and spreads on some accounts are wider than in the European day.

The London open (08:00 UK) brings the first genuine surge of volume. Price frequently breaks out of the overnight range, sometimes after a false start in the opposite direction, and the first two to three hours often set the tone for the day.

The London–New York overlap (roughly 13:00 to 16:30 UK) is when both major centres trade at once. It frequently brings the day's deepest liquidity and its second burst of direction, with US economic data typically landing at 13:30 UK.

Session choice is cost control with a clock on it

Tight spreads come from deep liquidity. Worthwhile moves come from active participation. Both cluster in the same few hours. Scalping a quiet session means paying the full toll for a market going nowhere; scalping the busy hours means the same toll buys more movement per trade.

This course trades two windows, and you choose one of them to start:

  • London window: 08:00 to 10:30 UK.
  • Overlap window: 13:00 to 15:30 UK.

Choosing a window means choosing fixed working hours and refusing to trade outside them. The scalper who "just has a quick look" at 21:00 is trading a thinner, more expensive market with a tired brain — three separate mistakes in one dressing gown.

KEY POINT

Pick one window and treat its start and end times as part of the strategy. A setup outside your window is not your setup.

The first fifteen minutes of a session deserve special care. Spreads are often still settling, slippage is at its worst, and the first push is frequently a stop run rather than the day's direction. Our plan needs an M5 trend with stacked moving averages and a pullback (Module 2), so in practice it rarely triggers in the first fifteen minutes anyway. That is a feature, not a bug.

Choosing the pair: the spread-to-movement test

Given Lesson 2, pair selection is barely a choice. You need the tightest spread, the deepest liquidity and reliable intraday movement. The test is mechanical: divide a typical 5-minute candle range during your window by the typical spread during that window. You want the market to move many multiples of its own spread inside your holding period.

Pair (illustrative, busy hours) Typical raw spread Typical M5 range Movement ÷ spread
EUR/USD 0.2 pips 4 pips 20x
USD/JPY 0.3 pips 5 pips 17x
GBP/USD 0.5 pips 6 pips 12x
EUR/GBP 0.6 pips 2.5 pips 4x
An exotic cross 4 pips 9 pips 2x

These numbers are illustrative — measure your own — but the ranking is typical. EUR/USD usually sits at the top for retail traders: the tightest spread and enormous liquidity. USD/JPY combines tight pricing with activity in both Asian and New York hours. GBP/USD moves more per candle at a wider spread, which is why its minimum stop under the 5x rule is larger. Beyond those three the case weakens quickly. An exotic cross can look exciting on the chart and still give you less movement per pip of toll than EUR/GBP.

One pair is enough. Two is defensible if their active hours differ. Watching five pairs on 1-minute charts is not diversification; it guarantees you are half-focused on everything.

COMMON MISTAKE

Choosing a pair because it "moves a lot". Movement only matters relative to the toll. A pair that moves 9 pips per candle with a 4-pip spread is a worse scalping market than one that moves 4 pips with a 0.2-pip spread.

The calendar is part of the session

Scheduled high-impact news sits inside your session like a speed bump in a bus lane. Central bank decisions, inflation prints and US employment data can move price 20 pips in seconds, with spreads widening sharply and stops filling well beyond their levels. For a 7.5-pip target, the release window is a cost catastrophe.

The rule writes itself:

  1. Check the economic calendar before every session.
  2. Mark every high-impact release for both currencies in your pair.
  3. Be flat 15 minutes before each release. Spreads often widen in anticipation.
  4. Do not trade again until 15 minutes after, and only once the spread is back to its normal reading — not merely when the candles look calmer.

Practice drill

Know your window's personality — with your own data

Sessions differ in character as well as volume, and your setup will not perform equally across them. A trend-pullback play may thrive in the London drive and struggle in the late-overlap drift. You cannot take this on trust from any course, including this one, because it varies by pair, by setup and by year. You have to measure it.

The method is simple and tedious, which is the correct combination. Timestamp every simulated trade. After a couple of hundred, break results out by half-hour. Most traders who do this honestly find their results are not evenly spread: a few half-hours carry the performance, several are noise, and one or two are actively destructive. Stop trading the destructive ones. Every trade you do not take in a bad half-hour is toll avoided and attention saved.

Going deeper

Daylight saving shifts the overlap. The UK and US change their clocks on different dates in spring and autumn. For a couple of weeks each year, New York opens an hour earlier relative to London, so the overlap and the 13:30 data release move to 12:30 UK. If your window is defined in UK time, re-check it in March and in late October.

Spread is a regime indicator. Your spread reading is a live measurement of liquidity. If your normal London-open spread is 0.2 pips and today it is sitting at 0.6, something is different — a holiday in one centre, a pending announcement, thin conditions. Treat any spread above your measured normal as a stand-down signal, not merely a cost.

Bank holidays and half-days. When London or New York is closed, the overlap does not really exist. Liquidity thins, ranges compress and spreads widen. Many scalpers simply do not trade those days, which removes a handful of the most expensive sessions of the year at a stroke.

USD/JPY in the overlap. For traders whose window is the afternoon, USD/JPY can be a sensible alternative to EUR/USD: it is active during US hours and responds cleanly to US data. Remember Lesson 2's point that its commission converts to more pips because the pip value is lower, and recalculate your minimum stop.

One pair per session, on purpose. It is tempting to watch EUR/USD and GBP/USD side by side to "double the opportunities". In practice the two are closely correlated during London hours, so the second chart mostly shows you the same setup twice, at a different cost, while splitting your attention in half. Two correlated positions are also one larger position in disguise. Pick the pair that passes your spread-to-movement test for the window, and give it all of your attention for the full session.

THE RULES
  • Trade one pair (two at most, only if their active hours differ) on raw-spread pricing
  • Trade only inside your chosen window: 08:00–10:30 UK or 13:00–15:30 UK
  • No trades in the first 15 minutes of the London window while spreads settle
  • Be flat 15 minutes before and stay flat until 15 minutes after any high-impact release for either currency
  • Stand down whenever the live spread is above your measured normal

Summary

  • The forex day has a pulse: a quiet Asian session, a London open surge and a London–New York overlap.
  • The scalper's toll is fixed, so trade only the windows where it buys the most movement: 08:00–10:30 or 13:00–15:30 UK.
  • Choose pairs by movement divided by spread; EUR/USD, USD/JPY and GBP/USD typically lead.
  • News releases are cost events: flat 15 minutes before, wait 15 minutes and a normal spread after.
  • Measure your own results by half-hour and stop trading the windows that do not work for your setup.

lessons.title: Steps 1 and 2 — Higher-Timeframe Bias and the EMA Trend Filter
lessons.summary: Set a one-direction bias from the H1 chart, check there is room to trade, and confirm it with the M5 20/50 EMA filter before you look for any entry.
lessons.html:
Most scalping losses are not caused by bad entries. They are caused by good-looking entries in the wrong direction, or in a market with no direction at all. On a 5-minute chart, almost anything can be made to look like a setup if you squint. The first two steps of the plan exist to stop you squinting.

Step 1 decides which way you are allowed to trade today, using the 1-hour chart. Step 2 checks that the 5-minute chart agrees, using two exponential moving averages. Only when both say the same thing do you move on to Step 3 and start looking for a trigger. If either says "no", the correct number of trades is zero, and that is a perfectly good session.

The four steps, in one line each

Before we start, here is the whole plan so you can see where these two steps sit:

  1. Bias (H1): decide long-only, short-only, or no trading.
  2. Trend filter (M5): the 20 EMA and 50 EMA must be stacked and sloping in the bias direction.
  3. Pullback trigger (M5): price pulls back into the 20–50 EMA band and prints a trigger candle back in the trend direction.
  4. Fixed-R exits: stop beyond the pullback, target at 1.5R, both set at entry.

Steps 1 and 2 are filters: they remove trades. Step 3 is the only step that creates one. That order matters. A trader who starts with the trigger and then looks for reasons to accept it will always find them.

Step 1 — The H1 bias

Before your window opens, look at the 1-hour chart of your pair with a 50-period EMA. You are answering one question: which direction has the structure been moving, and is price on the right side of the average?

Long-only bias requires both:

  • The last H1 candle closed above the H1 50 EMA.
  • The H1 swing structure is rising: the most recent swing high is above the one before, and the most recent swing low is above the one before (higher highs and higher lows).

Short-only bias is the mirror: close below the H1 50 EMA, with lower highs and lower lows.

Anything else is no bias. Price above the average but structure making lower highs? No bias. Higher highs but price sitting on the average? No bias. No bias means no trades in your window today. You do not "trade both ways and see".

Why the 1-hour chart? Because it is high enough to smooth out the noise of the 5-minute chart but low enough to reflect the current day's flow. A daily chart bias is often too slow — the daily trend can be up while the last eight hours have been a firm sell-off. A 15-minute bias is too fast; it flips several times a session and becomes the same noise you are trying to filter.

The room check

One more test belongs in Step 1. Mark the nearest H1 levels in the direction of your bias: the previous day's high, the most recent H1 swing high, and any round number ending in 00 or 50. If the nearest of those is closer than twice your typical target — about 15 pips on EUR/USD with a 7.5-pip target — there is not enough room for the scalp to work before it runs into a level where sellers have reason to appear.

This is not a prediction that price will reverse there. It is a cost judgement. A trade that has to break through a major level to reach its target is a lower-probability trade paying the same full toll.

KEY POINT

Step 1 removes half of all possible trades before the window opens: you trade one direction, or none. Most scalping damage happens on the other half.

Step 2 — The M5 EMA trend filter

Now drop to the 5-minute chart with a 20 EMA and a 50 EMA. The H1 bias said "long-only". The filter asks whether the 5-minute market is actually trending up right now, or whether the higher-timeframe story has paused.

For longs, all four conditions must hold:

  1. The 20 EMA is above the 50 EMA.
  2. Both are sloping up — each is higher than it was six candles (30 minutes) ago.
  3. There is visible separation: on EUR/USD, at least 2 pips between the two averages. Averages that are touching are not stacked; they are tangled.
  4. Price has made a fresh M5 swing high within the last 12 candles (one hour). A trend that has not made a new high for an hour is at best resting.

For shorts, mirror every condition.

The four conditions do different jobs. Stacking tells you direction. Slope tells you the direction is current rather than historical. Separation tells you the trend has enough momentum to produce a pullback that ends, rather than a chop that wanders. And the fresh high tells you the buyers are still winning recently, not just on average.

Why the 20 and the 50? There is nothing magic about the numbers. The 20 EMA on M5 covers the last hundred minutes and responds quickly; the 50 covers roughly four hours and moves slowly. Together they describe "the trend of this session" and "the trend of the day so far". Other pairs of averages would work similarly. What matters is that you choose one pair and never change it mid-test.

When the two steps disagree

The most common situation is not a clean pass or a clean fail. It is disagreement: the H1 bias is long, but the 5-minute chart is falling, with the 20 EMA below the 50.

That is not a short signal. Shorting would be trading against your Step 1 bias. Nor is it a long signal — buying a falling 5-minute market because the hourly chart is up is the classic way to catch a pullback that turns into a reversal. It is a wait. The 5-minute chart may well turn back up, the averages restack, and the plan comes alive. Or the H1 bias may break. Either way, the market will tell you; you do not have to guess.

COMMON MISTAKE

Using the higher timeframe as a reason to buy a falling 5-minute chart — "the hourly is up, so this dip must be a buy." Sometimes it is. Often it is the first leg of the hourly trend ending. The filter exists precisely so you do not have to decide which.

Doing it in two minutes

None of this should take long. Before the window opens:

  1. Open H1. Is the last close above or below the 50 EMA? Are the last two swing highs and lows rising, falling or mixed? Write the bias: LONG, SHORT or NONE.
  2. Mark the nearest H1 levels in the bias direction. Is there at least 15 pips of room (twice the target)? If not, write NONE.
  3. During the window, before each candidate: on M5, are the averages stacked, sloping, separated, with a fresh extreme in the last hour? Yes or no.

Write the bias on a sticky note on your screen. It is remarkably hard to take a short with "LONG ONLY" stuck to the monitor.

Going deeper

What the filter costs you. Every filter removes good trades as well as bad ones. Requiring a fresh M5 high within the hour will occasionally exclude the first pullback of a new trend, which can be the best one of the day. That is acceptable. A scalper does not need every good trade; it needs the trades it takes to be drawn from a cleaner population. Test any relaxation of the filter over at least 100 simulated trades before adopting it.

Bias changes during the session. If the H1 chart prints a close back below its 50 EMA during your window, the long bias is suspended for the rest of the session. Do not re-derive a short bias mid-session from the same chart that was bullish an hour ago; that is how traders end up flipping direction three times in a morning and paying the toll on each flip.

Regime awareness. The filter works best in sessions with directional flow — typically the London drive and the first part of the overlap. On days when the H1 chart is ranging inside a tight daily range (for example, the day before a major central bank decision), you will see Step 1 return NONE more often. That is the plan doing its job: the correct response to a market with no intraday direction is not a cleverer setup but fewer trades.

Why not more indicators? Adding RSI, MACD or a third average does not make the filter more accurate; it makes it slower to read and easier to rationalise. Two averages and one structure check, readable in seconds, beat a dashboard you have to interpret.

THE RULES
  • Bias from H1 only: long-only above the 50 EMA with higher highs and higher lows; short-only below with lower highs and lower lows; otherwise no trading
  • No trade if the nearest H1 level in the bias direction is closer than twice your target
  • M5 filter for longs: 20 EMA above 50 EMA, both rising over six candles, at least 2 pips apart (EUR/USD), fresh swing high within 12 candles — mirror for shorts
  • If H1 bias and M5 filter disagree, wait — never trade against either
  • If the H1 bias breaks during the session, stop for the rest of the session

Summary

  • Steps 1 and 2 are filters that remove trades; only Step 3 creates them.
  • H1 bias: above the 50 EMA with HH/HL for long-only, the mirror for short-only, anything else means no trades.
  • The room check rejects trades with less than twice the target distance to the next H1 level.
  • M5 filter: 20 over 50, both sloping, separated, with a fresh extreme in the last hour.
  • When H1 and M5 disagree, the plan waits; it never trades against either.

Buys because the H1 is bullish

Keep taking longs; bias was set this morning
Stop trading for the rest of the session
Move to the 1-minute chart
quiz.why: The bias is suspended once its condition breaks. Re-deriving the opposite bias mid-session leads to flip-flopping and paying the toll on each flip.

lessons.title: Step 3 — The Pullback Trigger
lessons.summary: Identify a valid pullback into the 20–50 EMA value band, recognise the three trigger candles, and place a stop-entry order that only fills if the market confirms.
lessons.html:
Steps 1 and 2 told you which direction you may trade and confirmed the 5-minute trend agrees. They have not given you a single trade. Step 3 is where the plan finally asks the market to do something specific — pull back, pause, and turn — and only then commits money.

The idea is old and simple: in an established trend, buy the dips (or sell the rallies) rather than the breakouts. What makes it a scalping method rather than a slogan is precision. Where exactly is the dip? What exactly counts as the turn? Where does the order go, and what cancels it? This lesson answers each of those questions with a rule you could hand to someone else and get the same result.

The value band

On the 5-minute chart, the area between the 20 EMA and the 50 EMA is the value band. In a healthy trend, price tends to spend most of its time above the 20 EMA (for longs), dip towards or into the band during pullbacks, and resume.

A pullback qualifies for the plan when:

  1. At least two candles have moved against the trend since the last swing high (for longs).
  2. A candle's low has touched or entered the band — at or below the 20 EMA.
  3. No candle has closed below the 50 EMA.

The third condition is the line in the sand. Wicks below the 50 EMA are tolerated; a close below it means the pullback has become something larger, and the setup is void. You then need the full Step 2 filter to reset — including a fresh swing high — before the plan is live again.

Why the band and not a fixed number of pips? Because the band adapts. On a fast morning the averages spread apart and the band widens; on a slower one it narrows. A rule like "buy a 10-pip dip" is far too deep on a quiet day and far too shallow on a busy one.

KEY POINT

Price must reach the value band without closing beyond the 50 EMA. Touching the band qualifies the pullback; closing through the far side cancels it.

The three trigger candles

Once a qualifying pullback is in place, you wait for a candle that closes back in the direction of the trend. The plan recognises three, and only three, trigger types.

1. Engulfing candle. A candle in the trend direction whose body completely covers the body of the previous counter-trend candle. For longs: it opens at or below the prior close and closes above the prior open. It shows the buyers absorbed everything the last candle's sellers offered and then some.

2. Rejection pin bar. A candle with a wick against the trend at least twice the length of its body, closing in the third of its range nearest the trend direction. For longs, a long lower wick that dipped into the band and a close near the top. It shows a probe that found no follow-through.

3. Momentum close. A candle in the trend direction that closes beyond the previous candle's extreme — above the prior high, for longs. Less dramatic than the first two, but it is the most common way pullbacks end on a 5-minute chart.

Anything else — a doji, an inside candle, a small candle that closes up but not through the previous high — is not a trigger. It might be the start of one. You wait for the next candle.

The order: a stop-entry beyond the trigger

The trigger candle does not put you in the trade. It tells you where to put the order.

  • Entry: a buy-stop order 0.2 pips above the trigger candle's high (sell-stop 0.2 below the low, for shorts).
  • Expiry: if the order has not filled within two candles (ten minutes), cancel it.
  • Stop: 1 pip below the lowest point of the pullback, including the trigger candle. If that is closer than your minimum (5 pips on EUR/USD at a 1.0-pip toll), widen it to the minimum and size down. If it is further than your maximum (8 pips on EUR/USD), skip the trade.
  • Target: 1.5R from the fill, set at entry. Lesson 6 covers why this does not move.

The stop-entry is deliberate. It means the market has to prove the turn by trading through the trigger candle's high before you are involved. If the trigger fails immediately and price rolls over, your order never fills and the trade costs you nothing. That filter alone removes a good share of the triggers that would have been losers — at the cost of a slightly worse entry price on the ones that work, and a little slippage on fast candles. Lesson 7 looks at the alternatives.

A valid trade that loses

Here is the same setup on a different morning. Every rule was followed.

There is no lesson to extract from this chart except the most important one in scalping: a valid losing trade is not a mistake. If you start adjusting the rules after trades like this — waiting for two triggers instead of one, moving the stop wider, skipping the next setup because "it's not working today" — you will be optimising your method against noise. Losers like this are the cost of doing business; they belong in the journal with an A grade.

COMMON MISTAKE

Judging a trigger by its outcome. A trader who takes ten valid trades and loses five has followed the plan perfectly. A trader who skips three valid trades because the previous two lost has quietly invented a new, untested strategy.

An invalid setup — the pullback that went too far

Now a case where the plan says no before any trigger appears.

This is where many traders lose money with a method like this one. They see the bullish candle, remember that "pullbacks in uptrends are buying opportunities", and buy. But the plan's definition of a pullback has an edge, and price has gone over it. What remains is a market that may be turning, and a trader who is guessing.

The anatomy of a short

Everything mirrors for shorts. Bias short on H1, M5 20 EMA below the 50 and falling, a rally of at least two candles whose high touches or enters the band, no close above the 50 EMA, and a bearish engulfing, upper-wick pin bar or close below the prior candle's low. Sell-stop 0.2 pips below the trigger low, stop 1 pip above the rally high (minimum and maximum applied), target 1.5R.

Practice drill

Going deeper

Why a stop-entry rather than entering at the close? Entering at the trigger close gives a better price — typically 1 to 2 pips on EUR/USD — but includes every trigger that fails on the very next candle. The stop-entry excludes those at the cost of the better price and some slippage. Which is better is an empirical question for your pair and window. As a starting point, the stop-entry is easier to execute consistently, and consistency is worth more than a pip in the first few hundred trades.

Depth of pullback is information. A pullback that just kisses the 20 EMA in a strong trend is different from one that sinks to the 50. Shallow pullbacks tend to resume quickly but give tighter structural stops (often widened to the minimum). Deep pullbacks give more room but are closer to invalidation. Log the depth — "20", "mid-band" or "50" — on every trade. After a couple of hundred trades you may find one depth carries most of your results.

Second triggers. If the first trigger's order expires unfilled and price continues to pull back within the band, a second trigger can form. The plan allows it provided every condition still holds. It does not allow a third: by then the pullback has lasted long enough that the "fresh high in the last hour" condition is usually failing anyway.

Time-of-session effects. Triggers in the first 45 minutes of a window often resolve faster — in both directions — than triggers late in the window, when momentum fades. If your journal shows late-window triggers drifting without reaching either stop or target, Lesson 9's time stop is designed for exactly that.

THE RULES
  • Pullback: at least two counter-trend candles, a low (or high, for shorts) touching or entering the 20–50 EMA band
  • A close beyond the 50 EMA voids the setup until the Step 2 filter fully resets
  • Valid triggers only: engulfing, rejection pin bar (wick at least 2x body, close in the outer third), or a close beyond the prior candle's extreme
  • Entry: stop order 0.2 pips beyond the trigger candle; cancel if unfilled after two candles
  • Stop: 1 pip beyond the pullback extreme, widened to your minimum if closer, trade skipped if beyond your maximum
  • Target: 1.5R from the fill, set at entry

Summary

  • The value band between the 20 and 50 EMA is where the plan looks for pullbacks to end.
  • A pullback must touch the band and must not close beyond the 50 EMA.
  • Three triggers only: engulfing, rejection pin bar and momentum close.
  • Enter on a stop order beyond the trigger; the market has to confirm the turn before you are in.
  • Valid losers are part of the method; invalid setups are refused before a trigger appears.

quiz.q: In an M5 uptrend, price pulls back for four candles, wicks below the 50 EMA once, and closes every candle above it. Is the pullback still valid?
options: No — any trade below the 50 EMA voids it
Yes — wicks beyond the 50 EMA are tolerated; only a close beyond it voids the setup
Only if RSI is oversold
Only on GBP/USD
quiz.why: The rule is about closes. A wick shows a probe; a close beyond the 50 EMA shows the pullback has become something larger.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a valid trigger in this plan?
options: A bullish candle whose body engulfs the previous red body
A candle with a lower wick three times its body, closing near its high
A small green inside candle that closes below the previous high
A green candle closing above the previous candle's high
quiz.why: An inside candle that fails to close beyond the prior high is not one of the three triggers. Wait for the next candle.

quiz.q: A trigger candle's high is 1.08625. Where does the buy-stop entry go?
options: 1.08625 exactly
At the next candle's open
quiz.why: The entry goes 0.2 pips (0.00002) above the trigger high: 1.08627.

quiz.q: The pullback low is 1.08540 and your buy-stop fills at 1.08600 on EUR/USD (minimum stop 5 pips, maximum 8). Where is the stop?
options: 1.08530 — 1 pip below the low, a 7-pip stop
1.08550 — the 5-pip minimum

lessons.title: Step 4 — Fixed-R Exits: Stops and Targets on the 5-Minute Chart
lessons.summary: Place the stop beyond the sweep zone and inside your minimum–maximum band, size the position from it, and set a fixed 1.5R target that you never move.
lessons.html:
Entries get all the attention in trading education. Exits decide the results. A scalper with an average entry and disciplined, consistent exits has a measurable method. A scalper with brilliant entries and improvised exits has a collection of anecdotes.

Step 4 of the plan makes exits boring on purpose. The stop goes in a place defined by structure and constrained by cost. The target is a fixed multiple of the stop. Both are attached to the order at entry. Nothing is moved afterwards except under the narrow, pre-tested rules in Lesson 9. That rigidity is not because flexible exits can never work. It is because flexible exits cannot be measured, and a scalping method you cannot measure is a method you cannot trust.

Where the stop goes, and why

A stop is not a pain threshold. It is the price at which your trade idea is wrong. For a pullback long, the idea is "the pullback has ended and the trend is resuming." The clearest evidence that idea is wrong is price trading below the low of the pullback. So the stop goes beyond the pullback extreme, plus a small buffer for noise and spread: 1 pip on EUR/USD.

Then two constraints, both from Lesson 2:

  • Minimum stop = 5x your all-in round-trip cost. With a 1.0-pip toll, 5 pips. A structural stop closer than that is widened to the minimum, with position size reduced so the money at risk does not change.
  • Maximum stop = 8 pips on EUR/USD (scale for other pairs from your own measurements of their typical M5 range). A structure that needs more than that is a pullback too large and too slow for a scalp. You skip it.

The maximum exists because a 12-pip stop implies an 18-pip target at 1.5R, and an 18-pip move is no longer reliably available inside a two-hour window on most mornings. The trade has quietly turned into a day trade.

The sweep zone

There is one more adjustment, and it matters more on low timeframes than anywhere else. Obvious levels attract stops. A pullback low that sits a pip above a round number (any price ending in 00 or 50), a prior M5 swing low or the session open has a crowd of stops sitting just beneath it. Price has a well-documented habit of dipping through such levels by a pip or two, triggering those stops, and then continuing in the original direction.

The rule: if an obvious level sits within 2 pips beyond your stop, move the stop beyond that level by 1 pip — provided the result is still inside your maximum. If it is not, skip the trade.

KEY POINT

Stops belong beyond the place where everyone else's stops are, not alongside them. A pip or two of extra distance is cheap insurance against the most common low-timeframe event there is.

Notice the trade-off. The sweep-zone rule makes the stop wider, which makes the position smaller and the target further away. You will occasionally miss a target by a pip that a tighter stop would have hit. Over a few hundred trades, the testing question is simple: do the extra survivals outweigh the slightly longer targets? On most major pairs and sessions, with a 1.5R target, that is the typical finding — but measure it for yours.

Sizing from the stop

Your stop distance sets your position size, never the other way round. The formula:

Position size = (account × risk per trade) ÷ (stop in pips × pip value per lot)

An illustrative example. Account £10,000, risk 0.5% per trade = £50. Stop 7 pips. On EUR/USD a pip on one standard lot is worth $10, roughly £7.90 at an exchange rate of 1.27. So: £50 ÷ (7 × £7.90) = 0.90 lots.

If the next setup has a 5-pip stop, the size becomes 1.27 lots; the money at risk stays at £50. This is why we measure everything in R: each trade risks the same 1R in money regardless of its pip distance, so results are comparable trade to trade.

Two practical notes. First, pre-calculate a small table of sizes for stops from 5 to 8 pips, and keep it beside your screen. Doing division during a live trigger is how errors happen. Second, round down, never up.

The target: fixed at 1.5R

The target is 1.5 times the stop distance, measured from your actual fill, placed as a limit order at entry. A 5-pip stop gives a 7.5-pip target; an 8-pip stop gives 12.

Why 1.5R? Three reasons.

The cost arithmetic. With cost at 0.2R, the break-even win rate at 1R is 60%; at 1.5R it is 48%; at 2R, 40%. A 1R target asks for a win rate few methods sustain after costs.

The available move. M5 pullback trades in a two-hour window typically have a limited runway before the next pullback, level or session lull. Targets beyond about 2R start to require the trend to make a whole new leg inside your window. That happens, but less often, and the win rate falls accordingly.

Execution. The target is a limit order, which means it fills at your price or better — no slippage on your winners. Your stop is a stop order and can slip. A fixed limit target is one of the few places a scalper gets a guaranteed price, and it is worth using.

1.5R is a reasonable starting point, not a law. Test 1.2R, 1.5R and 2R on the same set of simulated setups and pick one. What you must not do is choose per trade.

Why the target never moves

Moving the target feels like optimisation. In practice it converts a fixed, testable exit into a discretionary one, made at the moment you are most excited and least objective. Three things happen to traders who move targets:

  1. Some winners become larger. These are remembered vividly.
  2. Some winners become scratches or losers. These are explained away.
  3. The method's statistics become meaningless, because the exit rule changes with mood.

The third is the real damage. Lesson 11's journal and weekly review only work if each trade was managed the same way. A moved target is a trade from a different strategy — one you have never tested.

COMMON MISTAKE

Moving a target further away "because momentum is strong." Momentum at the moment of decision is visible to everyone, already reflected in price, and one candle from disappearing. If you believe larger targets work better, test 2R on a simulator for 100 trades. Do not test it live, one emotional trade at a time.

When the plan says skip

Skipping a trade that then works is one of the hardest things in scalping. It should not bother you. The plan is not trying to catch every move. It is trying to take only the trades whose size and shape it has been tested on. A skipped winner costs you nothing; a stretched rule costs you your statistics.

Going deeper

Stop orders slip; limit orders do not. In fast markets a stop-loss can fill beyond its level — perhaps 0.3 to 1 pip on a major in normal conditions, far more around news. That slippage belongs in your cost audit. If your log shows stop slippage creeping up, it usually means you are trading closer to releases or later into thin hours than you think.

Stop placement and the win rate. Every pip of extra stop room raises the win rate slightly (fewer noise stop-outs) and lowers the reward in pips per trade relative to account size (smaller position). The optimum is not "as tight as possible." For most M5 pullback setups the structural stop plus a 1-pip buffer, adjusted for sweep zones, sits near the sensible middle. Test the buffer between 0.5 and 2 pips on your own data before changing it.

What R hides. Measuring in R makes trades comparable, but it can hide position-size errors. If your journal shows a −1.4R loss on a trade with no slippage, you sized it wrongly. Add a column for "planned R versus realised R" and investigate every gap larger than 0.1R.

Partial targets. Some traders take half at 1R and the rest at 2R. It reduces variance per trade and changes the expectancy maths, usually slightly for the worse after costs (because the cost is paid on the full position while half the position earns less). Lesson 9 does the arithmetic. The default in this plan is one target.

THE RULES
  • Stop: 1 pip beyond the pullback extreme; widened to the minimum (5x cost) if closer; trade skipped if beyond the maximum (8 pips on EUR/USD)
  • If a round number, prior M5 swing or session level lies within 2 pips beyond the stop, place the stop 1 pip beyond that level — or skip if that exceeds the maximum
  • Size from the stop: risk a fixed fraction of the account (for example 0.5%) per trade; round size down
  • Target: 1.5R from the fill, entered as a limit order at the same time as the stop
  • Never move the target; never move the stop further away

Summary

  • The stop marks where the pullback idea is wrong: 1 pip beyond the pullback extreme, inside your minimum–maximum band.
  • Move stops beyond nearby obvious levels to avoid the sweep zone; skip if that breaks the maximum.
  • Size the position from the stop so every trade risks the same 1R in money.
  • The target is a fixed 1.5R limit order — measurable, slippage-free and never moved.
  • Skipping a setup that would have worked costs nothing; stretching a rule costs your statistics.

lessons.title: 1-Minute Execution — Refining the Entry Without Inventing a New Strategy
lessons.summary: Use the 1-minute chart only after the 5-minute setup is armed, trigger on a defined M1 structure shift, and execute every order with pre-set size, attached stops and a rehearsed emergency exit.
lessons.html:
The 1-minute chart is the most dangerous chart in retail trading. Not because it is noisy — though it is — but because it is persuasive. Every minute it produces a new pattern, a new swing, a new reason. Traders who live on it end up with a different strategy every hour.

This course uses the 1-minute chart in exactly one way: as a zoom lens on a 5-minute setup that already exists. The 5-minute chart tells the story — bias, filter, pullback into the band. The 1-minute chart only times the entry within it. If the 5-minute chart has not armed the setup, the 1-minute chart is closed.

Used that way, the 1-minute refinement offers two real benefits: a better entry price on many trades, and fewer trades skipped for stops that are too wide. It also has real costs, and this lesson is honest about both. The second half covers the mechanical skill of execution itself — orders, platform, drills — which matters more on M1 than anywhere else.

When the 1-minute chart opens

The M1 refinement is only allowed when all of the following are already true on M5:

  1. H1 bias set (Step 1).
  2. M5 trend filter passing (Step 2).
  3. M5 price has entered the value band without closing beyond the 50 EMA — the setup is armed.

At that moment, and not before, look at the 1-minute chart. Then, from the same armed state, you have two entry methods to choose from — and you choose one in advance, for a whole block of testing, not per trade:

  • Standard (M5): wait for an M5 trigger candle and use the stop-entry from Lesson 5.
  • Refined (M1): wait for the M1 structure shift described below.

You never use both on the same setup, and you never switch between them because one "looks better" on a given morning.

The M1 structure shift

Zoomed in, an M5 pullback in an uptrend is usually a small downtrend on the 1-minute chart: lower highs and lower lows, drifting into the band. The pullback ends, on M1, when that micro downtrend breaks — when buyers push price through the most recent M1 lower high.

The rule, for longs:

  • Identify the most recent M1 lower high — the last swing high of the micro downtrend.
  • The trigger is an M1 candle that closes above it.
  • Entry: buy-stop 0.2 pips above that candle's high. Cancel if not filled within three M1 candles.
  • Stop: 1 pip below the lowest point of the pullback, exactly as in Lesson 6 — sweep-zone rule, minimum and maximum all unchanged.
  • Target: 1.5R from the fill.

What the refinement buys you

Look at the numbers in that chart. With the standard M5 entry, the buy-stop above the M5 trigger candle would have filled around 8.2. The pullback low (with buffer) was 0.2, so the stop would have been 8 pips — right at the maximum — and the 1.5R target 12 pips away. With the M1 entry at 5.2, the same structural stop is 5 pips and the target 7.5 pips away.

The money at risk is identical — 1R either way, because position size adjusts. But the market has to travel less to pay you 1.5R. Over many trades that means:

  • Some trades that the M5 entry would have skipped (stop beyond the maximum) become takeable.
  • Some trades that would have stalled short of a 12-pip target reach a 7.5-pip one.

What the refinement costs you

There is no free lunch, and three costs come with the zoom.

More false starts. M1 structure shifts are frequent and many fail. An M1 trigger fires earlier than an M5 one, which means it fires on more pullbacks that were not actually finished.

Cost concentration. Better entries often produce stops right at your minimum. That is fine — the minimum exists for this — but you will be trading at the 0.2R cost ceiling more often, and every slippage pip weighs more.

Attention. Watching an M1 chart for a shift is far more demanding than waiting for an M5 candle to close. If your decision quality is already stretched by the end of a window, M1 work makes that worse. Lesson 11 has more on this.

So which should you use? The honest answer is: test both on the same few hundred armed setups — a simulator with replay makes this straightforward — and compare expectancy after costs, not win rate. Many traders find the M5 stop-entry is simpler to execute and nearly as good. Some find the M1 refinement materially better on their pair. Do not guess; measure.

KEY POINT

The 1-minute chart never creates a setup. It only refines the entry of a setup the 5-minute chart has already armed — and you choose M5 or M1 entries in advance for a whole testing block, never per trade.

The late-entry trap

One more failure mode deserves its own chart, because the 1-minute chart makes it so tempting.

The rule is simple: if price has already moved more than half the planned target distance from the pullback extreme when you would enter, the setup is missed. Missing setups is normal. Chasing them is how M1 traders turn a tested method into an improvisation.

Execution is a physical skill

Everything above is thinking. Now hands. On the 1-minute chart, mechanical execution — how fast and accurately you turn a decision into a working order — materially affects results. Three seconds of fumbling on a 5-pip stop can be half a pip of slippage, which is 0.1R.

Orders. Know the trade-offs cold:

  • A market order guarantees a fill, not a price. Fastest, but every fill in a fast market carries slippage.
  • A limit order guarantees a price, not a fill. Zero entry slippage, but you will sometimes miss trades.
  • A stop-entry order fills only if price trades through your level — which is why the plan uses it. It confirms the turn, but it fires into momentum, so some slippage is normal.

The plan uses stop-entry orders for entries and stop-losses, and a limit order for the target. That combination is decided once. You do not choose order types during a trade.

The platform as a cockpit. Strip your screen to the objects that inform or execute a decision: the M5 chart (with the two EMAs and your marked levels), the M1 chart beside it, a one-click order panel with pre-set size, and a live spread readout. No news feed, no chat room, no extra pairs, no indicators you do not use. Every extra object is a tax on recognition speed.

Safety rails, set while calm. Default size locked to your sizing table. Stop and target attached automatically to every entry (most platforms support bracket or OCO orders). One-click close enabled and practised. A daily loss cut-off configured if your platform offers one.

The drills. On a demo account, practise the full cycle — read the trigger, place the bracket order, confirm it is working — until it takes under five seconds without looking for buttons. Practise the emergency flatten until it is reflexive. And write your broker's dealing-desk phone number and your account number on paper beside the screen, because the moment your platform freezes with a position open is not the moment to search for them.

COMMON MISTAKE

Holding a "mental stop" on the 1-minute chart. On a fast timeframe, a mental stop is a plan to negotiate with yourself in the middle of a losing trade. The stop is attached in the platform at entry, every time.

Going deeper

Latency, honestly. Retail scalping does not compete with high-frequency firms on speed and does not need to. A wired connection, a platform that stays responsive during busy periods (test it during a news release while flat), and a broker whose fills you have measured are enough. A VPS near your broker's server is a reasonable step only if your logs show latency-related slippage.

Why three M1 candles for expiry? An M1 shift that does not follow through within three minutes is usually a pause, not a turn. Waiting longer means you are filled late into a move that may already be stalling. Test two to five candles if you like, but fix the number.

Two charts, one decision. Some traders find watching M5 and M1 together splits their attention. An alternative is to set an alert at the M5 20 EMA: when it fires, the setup may be arming, and only then do you look closely. That keeps the M1 chart closed for most of the session.

Combining refinements is a new strategy. M1 shift plus candle trigger plus a limit at the band plus... Each addition creates a different method with its own statistics. If you want to test a variation, test it as a separate block of trades. Never blend them in live trading.

THE RULES
  • The M1 chart opens only after the M5 setup is armed (bias, filter, price in the band without closing beyond the 50 EMA)
  • Choose M5 stop-entry or M1 shift entry in advance for a whole testing block — never per trade
  • M1 trigger: a close beyond the last M1 lower high (higher low for shorts); stop-entry 0.2 pips beyond that candle, cancelled after three M1 candles
  • Stops and targets follow Lesson 6 unchanged: structural stop, sweep-zone rule, minimum and maximum, 1.5R target
  • If price has travelled more than half the target distance from the pullback extreme, the setup is missed — do not chase
  • Every entry goes in as a bracket: stop and target attached at the moment of entry

Summary

  • The 1-minute chart only refines entries for setups the 5-minute chart has armed.
  • The M1 structure shift — a close beyond the last micro lower high — often gives a better price and a smaller pip stop.
  • It costs more false starts, more trades at the cost ceiling and more attention; test it against the M5 entry rather than assuming.
  • Do not chase: more than half the target distance from the pullback extreme means the setup has gone.
  • Execution is a drilled physical skill: pre-chosen order types, bracket orders, a cockpit screen and a rehearsed emergency exit.

It removes the need for a stop
It doubles the target

Stop-entry, attached stop-loss, limit target
