options: The M1 rule is broken and should be abandoned
It was a valid loss: earlier triggers fire on more unfinished pullbacks
The stop should have been moved lower after entry
They should have used both M1 and M5 entries
quiz.why: The trade followed the rules. Earlier triggers accept more false starts; that cost is weighed over hundreds of trades, not one.

lessons.title: Candle Triggers at Micro Levels
lessons.summary: Mark the five or six intraday levels that matter before the session, read the plan's three trigger candles where those levels meet the value band, and skip triggers that have no room to reach their target.
lessons.html:
A pin bar in the middle of nowhere and a pin bar resting on the overnight high are the same shape. They are not the same event. The first tells you a few sellers ran out of interest for five minutes. The second tells you that price came back to a place every intraday participant could see, tested it, and was refused.

Lesson 5 gave you three trigger candles and the value band where they count. This lesson adds location. It shows you which handful of intraday levels are worth marking, how to mark them before the session rather than during it, and how they change two things about a setup: how much you trust the trigger, and whether the trade has room to reach its target at all. It does not add a new setup. The four-step plan is unchanged. Levels make it sharper, and occasionally they veto it.

The levels that matter when minutes matter

Forget the weekly trend lines. On the 1- and 5-minute charts, price is organised by humbler, nearer levels — the ones every intraday trader has on their screen:

  • The prior day's high and low. The most widely watched intraday reference there is.
  • The Asian range high and low. For European pairs, the boundaries of the quiet overnight session. London often tests or breaks one of them early.
  • Round numbers. Prices ending in 00 and, to a lesser degree, 50. Orders cluster there because humans like tidy numbers.
  • The day's opening price. Some traders also mark the London open price at 08:00.
  • Any level already fought over twice today. If price has turned from the same area twice, the third visit is worth noticing.

That is the whole list. Mark these before the session starts — at 07:45 for the London window, 12:45 for the overlap — and stop there. Five or six lines is plenty. If everything is marked, nothing is, and a scalper drawing lines mid-session is a scalper not watching price.

Why levels work — without the mysticism

A level is useful to a scalper because of crowding, not magic. When many participants put stops and entries around the same obvious price, that neighbourhood becomes predictable in a narrow way. Price tends to speed up as it approaches (stops being triggered), often overshoots by a pip or two (the cluster being cleared), and then shows its hand: either it carries on with real follow-through, or it snaps back once the forced orders are used up.

That is all we need to believe. We do not need a story about who is behind the move. The chart observably shows price behaving differently near widely watched prices; the plan uses that behaviour and nothing more.

KEY POINT

A level does not create a trade. It tells you where the plan's own trigger is most worth trusting — and where a target is likely to run into a wall.

Job one: grading the location

When a qualifying pullback into the 20–50 EMA band also lands on a pre-marked level, two separate reasons to expect support (or resistance) are in the same place. We call that confluence, and it is the best location the plan can offer.

The rules for using it are deliberately modest:

  1. Confluence is preferred, not required. A valid trigger in the band without a level is still a valid trade under the plan. The passport says "ideally at a pre-marked micro level" for a reason: requiring a level would cut the number of setups sharply, and you have no evidence yet that it improves results.
  2. Log it. Add a column to your journal — "L" if the pullback extreme was within 2 pips of a pre-marked level, blank if not. After a couple of hundred trades you will know whether the confluence trades carry more of your results. Many traders find they do. Some find no difference. Measure, then decide.

Read that chart in the plan's order, not the level's. Bias long. Filter passing: the 20 EMA above the 50, both rising, a fresh high inside the hour. Pullback: four counter-trend candles, a low inside the band, no close below the 50 EMA. Trigger: a pin bar with a lower wick about sixteen times its body, closing in the top third of its range. Only then does the level add anything: the wick turned at a price the whole market had marked. Same trade, more reason to trust it.

Reading the trigger candle at a level

The three triggers have not changed — engulfing, rejection pin bar, momentum close. What a level adds is a way to read them more precisely.

The wick tells you where the test happened. A pin bar whose wick reaches into or slightly through a level, then closes back on the trend side, has tested the level and been refused. A pin bar whose wick stops three pips short of the level has not tested it at all — the level may still be waiting below.

A small overshoot is normal. Because stops cluster just beyond obvious prices, a wick that pierces a level by a pip or two and closes back is often a stronger sign than one that stops neatly on it. The stops were taken, and price still could not continue.

Bodies tell you about conviction. A trigger candle with a full body that closes near its extreme, followed by a shallow pause, shows genuine participation. A cluster of small overlapping candles with long wicks on both sides, sitting on a level, shows a market that has not made up its mind. That is not a trigger. Wait for one of the three to print, or let the setup expire.

The sweep and reclaim on the 1-minute chart

If you are running the M1 refinement block from Lesson 7, levels show up in a specific shape: price knifes through the level, often in a single 1-minute candle, and closes back above it (for longs) within that candle or the next. On the 5-minute chart, the same event usually appears as a pin bar into the level.

The sweep is information, not a trigger. Your M1 trigger is still the structure shift: an M1 close above the last lower high. Often the reclaim candle or the one after it produces that shift within a minute or two, which is why the two are worth recognising together.

COMMON MISTAKE

Buying the sweep candle itself, mid-wick, because "the stops have been taken". Sometimes they have, and price keeps falling anyway because the level simply broke. The plan waits for the close back above the level and a defined trigger, and accepts a slightly worse price as the cost of knowing.

Job two: the room check

Here is the job that saves money. A level does not only support your entry; levels on the other side of the trade can block your target.

The rule: before entering, find the nearest pre-marked level in the direction of the trade. If it sits between your entry and your 1.5R target, skip the trade.

This is a micro version of the Lesson 4 rule about H1 levels. A target that has to break through the prior-day high, a round number or the Asian range boundary to be paid is a lower-probability target paying the same full toll. On a 7.5-pip target, it takes only one stubborn level to turn a sensible trade into a coin-flip with a 0.2R entry fee.

This is the failure mode of traders who have learned candle patterns well. The trigger is real; the trade is not. The room check takes about three seconds if your levels were marked before the session, and it is the main reason to mark them.

Two clarifications. First, a level slightly beyond your target does not block it; the target fills first. Second, do not "solve" a blocked target by shrinking it to fit beneath the level. A 1R target pays a 60% break-even win rate at 0.2R of cost, as Lesson 2 showed. The fix for a blocked target is to skip the trade.

Practice drill

Work through the plan in order before you reveal the answer. Bias is short. The levels were marked before the session.

Going deeper

Levels decay with use. A level that has been tested once and held is meaningful. A level that has been tested four times in a morning is usually being worn away: each test consumes the orders resting there. If price keeps returning to the same support, the fourth bounce is less trustworthy than the first, and a break becomes more likely. In your journal, note whether the level was on its first, second or third-plus test.

Round numbers are not all equal. On EUR/USD, a "big figure" ending in 00 tends to attract more orders than a 50, and a 50 more than a 20 or 80. Mark the 00s and 50s near current price and ignore the rest.

The level-to-stop relationship. Levels interact with Lesson 6's sweep-zone rule in both directions. A level inside your stop (between entry and stop, as in the Asian-high chart) is good: your stop sits beyond the crowd. A level just beyond your stop is a hazard, and the stop must move past it or the trade is skipped. Read both before the order goes in.

Why not trade levels on their own? Fading every touch of a level, without the trend filter, is a completely different strategy — a range-reversal method with its own statistics, costs and failure modes. It may work for some traders. It is not this plan, and blending the two is how one tested method becomes two untested ones.

Session timing changes level behaviour. Levels tested in the first 30 minutes of London tend to be swept more aggressively, because liquidity and stop density are both high. Levels tested late in the window are more often simply drifted through. If your journal shows confluence trades working early and failing late, that is a real finding — but wait for a sample of at least a hundred trades before acting on it.

THE RULES
  • Mark five or six levels before the session (prior-day high/low, Asian high/low, 00 and 50 round numbers, day open, any level fought over twice) — never during it
  • Levels grade a setup; they never create one. The four-step plan decides whether there is a trade
  • Log confluence ("L") when the pullback extreme is within 2 pips of a pre-marked level
  • Room check: if a pre-marked level sits between entry and the 1.5R target, skip the trade — do not shrink the target to fit
  • A sweep through a level is information; the trigger is still an engulfing, pin bar, momentum close (M5) or structure shift (M1)

Summary

  • The micro levels that organise intraday price are few: prior-day high and low, the Asian range, round numbers, the day's open and levels already fought over.
  • Mark them before the session; five or six is plenty.
  • A trigger at a level in the value band is the plan's best location, but confluence is preferred and logged, not required.
  • The room check skips any trade whose 1.5R target lies beyond a pre-marked opposing level.
  • A perfect candle at a perfect level is still no trade if bias, filter or pullback rules have failed.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT on the lesson's list of levels to mark before the session?
options: The prior day's high and low
The Asian range high and low
A trend line drawn on the weekly chart
Round numbers ending in 00 and 50
quiz.why: The scalper's levels are near, widely watched intraday prices. Weekly trend lines are not part of the micro-level map.

quiz.q: A valid M5 trigger appears in the value band, but there is no pre-marked level nearby. What does the plan do?
options: Skips it — confluence is required
Takes it — confluence is preferred and logged, not required
Takes it at half size
Waits for price to reach a level
quiz.why: A level grades a setup but is not part of the plan's conditions. Log whether confluence was present and let the data decide later.

quiz.q: Your buy-stop is at 1.08450 with a 5-pip stop. The prior-day high is at 1.08500. What does the room check say?
options: Trade — the level is above entry
Skip — the level sits between entry and the 1.5R target at 1.08525
Trade with a 0.9R target under the level
Move the stop to 4 pips
quiz.why: The 1.5R target is 7.5 pips away at 1.08525, and the level at 1.08500 blocks it. Skip; never shrink the target to fit.

quiz.q: In the 'swept and reclaimed' chart, what was the actual entry trigger?
options: The sweep candle's low
The candle closing back above 1.0900
The next M1 candle closing above the last lower high — the structure shift
A market order as soon as price touched 1.0900
quiz.why: The sweep and reclaim are information. The M1 trigger in this plan is still the structure shift, confirmed by a stop-entry.

quiz.q: In the GBP/USD drill, the pin bar sat perfectly on the Asian low inside the band. Why was it no trade?
options: Pin bars are not valid short triggers
The upper wick pierced the level
The 20 EMA had turned up, so the trend filter was no longer passing
GBP/USD is not an approved pair
quiz.why: The rally turned the 20 EMA, so it was no longer falling over six candles. A good candle at a good level never overrides the filter.

quiz.q: A support level has held four times this morning. How should you treat a fifth test?
options: As the strongest test yet
With more caution — repeated tests tend to wear a level away
As a guaranteed bounce
As irrelevant, since levels do not matter on M5
quiz.why: Each test consumes resting orders. Repeatedly tested levels become more likely to break, not less.

lessons.title: Trade Management — Partials, Break-Even Rules and What They Really Cost
lessons.summary: Know exactly what you may and may not do once a scalp is live, calculate what break-even stops, partial profits and time stops do to expectancy after costs, and test any of them as a separate block rather than improvising.
lessons.html:
Once a scalp is live, the hardest part of the trade is usually over. The decision has been made, the stop and target are attached, the size is right. What remains is the part where most scalpers lose their edge: the five to thirty minutes in which they watch price wobble around their entry and feel an overwhelming urge to do something.

This lesson is about that urge. It sets out the plan's default, which is to do almost nothing, then examines the three management techniques traders most often add — break-even stops, partial profits and time stops — with the arithmetic in the open. None of them is free. Each changes your expectancy in a way that depends on your costs and on how your trades tend to behave after entry. That makes them testable, and it makes improvising them in the moment a bad idea.

The default: set and leave

The plan's default management, from Lesson 6, is short enough to memorise:

  • Stop and target are attached as a bracket at entry.
  • The target never moves.
  • The stop never moves further away.
  • You do not add to the position.
  • You do not close early because of a feeling.

That leaves exactly three things you may do while a trade is open, and only if they were decided before the session:

  1. A tested break-even rule, if you have adopted one for this block of trades.
  2. A tested time stop, if you have adopted one for this block.
  3. An abnormality exit: closing at market because something has broken — the platform is freezing, the spread has blown out to several times normal, or an unscheduled shock is moving price violently. This is an emergency procedure, not a trading decision.

Everything else is watching. If you find watching unbearable, a common professional answer is to stop watching: once the bracket is confirmed, look at the M5 chart only at candle closes, or minimise the order panel entirely.

KEY POINT

In this plan, trade management is decided before the session, not during the trade. Anything you would do to a live trade must be a written rule you have tested on a whole block of trades.

Break-even stops: the scratch is not free

The most popular management rule in retail trading is "move the stop to break-even once the trade is 1R in profit". It feels like a free option: once you are at entry, you cannot lose.

For a scalper that is not quite true, for two reasons.

First, break-even is not zero. A stop at your entry price still pays the toll. With a 1.0-pip round-trip cost on a 5-pip stop, a "break-even" exit is a loss of 0.2R. A true break-even, where you lose nothing, would mean a stop one pip above entry — which is even closer to price and gets hit even more often.

Second, it converts some winners as well as some losers. A stop at entry is very close to price. On the 5-minute chart, pullbacks of 5 pips inside a trade that eventually works are routine. Every one of those becomes a scratch.

The break-even arithmetic

The only trades a break-even rule affects are the ones that reach +1R and then come all the way back to entry. Call the share of those trades that would have gone on to hit the target p. Without the rule, each of those trades is worth, on average:

p × 1.3R − (1 − p) × 1.2R

With the rule, every one of them is worth −0.2R. Setting the two equal gives p = 0.4. So, with this plan's numbers:

  • If fewer than 40% of your "back-to-entry" trades would have gone on to the target, the break-even rule helps.
  • If more than 40% would have, the rule is quietly costing you money.

A hypothetical illustration: out of 100 trades, 20 reach +1R and then return to entry. If 10 of those 20 would have gone on to win, the rule turns +1.0R (10 × 1.3 − 10 × 1.2) into −4.0R (20 × −0.2). That is a 5R swing per hundred trades, which on a thin scalping edge can be the entire edge. If only 4 of the 20 would have won, the rule turns −14.0R into −4.0R and saves 10R. Same rule, opposite verdict. These numbers are invented to show the mechanism, not a claim about any strategy.

You can measure p on a simulator without ever using the rule: for each trade, log whether it reached +1R and whether it later touched entry. That is one extra column and it answers the question with your own data.

COMMON MISTAKE

Moving to break-even "when it feels like it might turn". An undefined break-even rule combines the costs of the real one with the inconsistency of discretion. It is the worst of both, and it makes your journal unreadable.

Partial profits: smoother, not better

The second popular technique is to close part of the position early — for example half at 1R — and let the rest run to a further target such as 2R.

Here is the arithmetic, with the same 0.2R toll paid on the full position:

What happens Single 1.5R target Half at 1R, half at 2R
Stopped before +1R −1.2R −1.2R
Reaches +1R, then stopped −1.2R −0.2R
Reaches 1.5R, not 2R, then stopped +1.3R −0.2R
Reaches +2R +1.3R +1.3R

Look at the bottom row first. The best possible partial-profit trade pays exactly what the single 1.5R target pays — but it needs price to travel 10 pips on a 5-pip stop instead of 7.5. The partial version is better in the second row, worse in the third. Whether it helps overall depends on how often your trades stall between 1R and 1.5R compared with how often they run between 1.5R and 2R.

What partials reliably do is reduce variance: fewer full losses, fewer full wins, a smoother equity curve. That can be valuable for your psychology. It is not automatically valuable for your expectancy, and on a 5-pip stop there is a practical cost too: splitting a 0.9-lot position into two halves is fine, but smaller accounts quickly hit minimum lot sizes and rounding.

Time stops: closing the trade that is going nowhere

The third technique is the one this plan offers as an option in the passport: if the trade is not at least +0.5R in profit after six M5 candles (30 minutes), close it at market.

The logic comes from what a pullback scalp is. The idea is that the pullback has ended and the trend is resuming. Trends that resume do so with some urgency; most of this plan's winners spend very little time near entry. A trade that is still sitting around its entry half an hour later has not been proven wrong, but its premise is fading, and it is tying up your attention and your risk while the window runs down.

The time stop is not free either. Its exits pay the toll, and some slow starters would have gone on to win. In practice, traders who test it usually find it reduces the number of full −1.2R losses and slightly reduces the number of winners. Whether that trade-off is positive is, again, an empirical question. That is why the passport calls it optional and tested.

Fix its parameters before you test it — six candles and +0.5R are a reasonable start — and do not tune them on fewer than a couple of hundred trades. Shaving the numbers until last week's results look perfect is curve-fitting, not testing.

How to test a management rule properly

Every technique in this lesson follows the same test procedure.

  1. Collect a block of armed, triggered setups on a simulator — ideally the same few hundred, replayed.
  2. Run them under the default plan and log the result of each in R after costs.
  3. Run the identical setups under the alternative rule — break-even at +1R, partials, or the time stop — and log those results too.
  4. Compare expectancy in R, not win rate. Break-even rules and time stops nearly always raise the win rate (scratches feel like non-losses), while sometimes lowering expectancy. The number that pays you is expectancy.
  5. Choose one version and use it for the next live block. Do not switch per trade.

Note that the comparison is fair only because the entries are identical. Testing a management rule on different trades from the ones you tested the default on tells you about the trades, not the rule.

Going deeper

Why management rules look better than they are. Every management rule feels good in the moment it saves you: the break-even stop that dodged a full loss, the time stop that exited before the collapse. The trades it costs you are invisible, because you were not in them when they went on to work. That asymmetry of memory is exactly why these rules have to be measured on a log, and why the default in this plan is to leave the trade alone.

Trailing stops on a 1.5R target are mostly noise. Trailing a stop behind each M1 swing on a 7.5-pip target means trailing inside the spread-and-noise zone. In practice it behaves like a tight break-even rule with extra discretion. If you want to test trailing, test it with a larger target and treat it as a different strategy.

Abnormality exits must stay rare. If your journal shows "abnormality exit" more than once or twice a month, you are either trading too close to news, using a platform you cannot rely on, or using the label to disguise discretionary exits. Each case needs fixing at its source.

Don't confuse management with re-entry. If a trade is stopped and a fresh, complete setup forms later in the window, that is a new trade under the full checklist, counted against your trade cap and consecutive-loss breaker in Lesson 10. "Getting back in" a stopped trade on the next candle is not management. It is the opening move of tilt, which Lesson 11 deals with.

THE RULES
  • Default: bracket attached at entry; never move the target; never widen the stop; never add; never close on a feeling
  • Break-even, partials and time stops are optional and decided per testing block — never per trade
  • A break-even stop at entry still costs the toll (about 0.2R); count it as a loss in the journal
  • Optional time stop: close at market if not at +0.5R after six M5 candles
  • Abnormality exit only for platform failure, a spread blow-out or an unscheduled shock — log the reason every time
  • Compare management rules on identical setups by expectancy in R after costs, not by win rate

Summary

  • Once a scalp is live, the plan's default is to leave it alone: the bracket does the work.
  • A break-even stop at entry costs about 0.2R and converts some winners as well as some losers; with this plan's numbers it helps only if fewer than 40% of back-to-entry trades would have won.
  • Partials at 1R and 2R pay the same maximum as a single 1.5R target but need a longer move; they smooth variance rather than reliably adding edge.
  • A six-candle time stop cuts dead trades early at the cost of some slow winners; test it before using it.
  • Test every management rule on the same setups, compare expectancy in R, then commit to one version for a whole block.

quiz.q: Your all-in cost is 1.0 pip and your stop is 5 pips. You move your stop to entry and it is hit. What is the result in R?
options: 0R — break-even
quiz.why: Exiting at the entry price still pays the round-trip toll: 1.0 ÷ 5 = 0.2R. 'Break-even' is a small loss for a scalper.

quiz.q: Using this plan's numbers, when does a break-even rule at +1R improve expectancy?
options: Always — it removes risk
When fewer than 40% of trades that return to entry would have gone on to hit target
When more than 60% of trades are winners
Never
quiz.why: Without the rule those trades are worth p × 1.3 − (1 − p) × 1.2; with it, −0.2R. The two are equal at p = 0.4.

quiz.q: Compared with a single 1.5R target, what does closing half at 1R and half at 2R do to the best possible outcome after costs?
options: Raises it to +1.8R
Leaves it at +1.3R, but price must travel to 2R to earn it
Lowers it to +0.8R
Removes the toll
quiz.why: 0.5 × 1R + 0.5 × 2R − 0.2R = +1.3R, the same as a single 1.5R target after costs, but it needs a 10-pip move on a 5-pip stop instead of 7.5.

quiz.q: In the time-stop chart, the trade was closed after six candles and later the original stop was hit. What is the right conclusion?
options: Time stops always improve results
This trade was helped; others will be cut before they win, so the rule must be tested over a block
The target should have been moved closer
The trade should never have been taken
quiz.why: Single outcomes prove nothing. Time stops trade fewer full losses for some lost slow winners; only a tested sample shows the net effect.

quiz.q: A trader adopts a break-even rule and sees their win rate rise from 50% to 58%. Is the rule working?
options: Yes — a higher win rate means more profit
Not necessarily — compare expectancy in R after costs, because scratches can raise win rate while lowering expectancy
Yes, if the sample is over 20 trades
No — break-even rules never work
quiz.why: Management rules commonly raise win rate by converting losses and winners into small scratches. Only expectancy in R tells you whether they pay.

quiz.q: Which of these is a legitimate reason to close a live scalp early under the plan?
options: Price has stalled and you feel nervous
You want to free up attention for another pair
The platform has started freezing and the spread has jumped to several times normal
The trade is +1.2R and you would like to lock it in
quiz.why: Only a pre-decided rule or a genuine abnormality justifies intervention. Nerves and the wish to lock in profit are the urges this lesson is designed to remove.

lessons.title: Daily Loss Limits, Trade Caps and the Consecutive-Loss Breaker
lessons.summary: Set the five numeric limits that govern every scalping session — daily loss limit, trade cap, consecutive-loss breaker, session clock and weekly limit — understand the variance that makes them necessary, and enforce them mechanically.
lessons.html:
Your stop-loss protects you from a single trade. Nothing in the four-step plan protects you from yourself across a morning. That is the job of this lesson.

Scalping compresses a month's worth of decisions into a couple of hours. A swing trader who has a bad week loses a few trades. A scalper who has a bad hour can take eight, each one faster and less considered than the last. The losses that end scalping careers are almost never one big trade. They are a sequence of ordinary ones taken after the trader should have stopped.

So the plan ends every session by rule, not by mood. There are five numbers. You write them down while calm, you enforce them mechanically where your platform allows, and you never renegotiate them while trading.

The five numbers

These are the plan's defaults. They are illustrative, sensible starting points, and you may adjust them at a weekly review — never during a session.

  1. Daily loss limit: −3R. Once the day's realised result reaches −3R or worse, you open no new trades. The session is over.
  2. Trade cap: 6 trades per session. The sixth trade is the last, whatever happens to it.
  3. Consecutive-loss breaker: 3. Three losing trades in a row ends the session, even if the daily limit has not been reached.
  4. The session clock. No new entries after the window closes — 10:30 UK for London, 15:30 for the overlap. Trades already open run to their bracket (or their time stop, if you use one).
  5. Weekly loss limit: −6R. Reach it and you stop live trading until your weekly review.

In money, with an illustrative £10,000 account risking 0.5% per trade, one R is £50. The daily limit is £150, or 1.5% of the account. Because the limit stops you opening trades rather than capping the loss exactly, and each full loss costs about 1.2R after costs, a realistic worst normal day is around −3.6R to −4R: roughly £180 to £200, or 2%. That is annoying. It is not dangerous. That is exactly the point: a maximum-loss day should be repairable by a couple of ordinary good days.

KEY POINT

The daily loss limit is the scalper's most important risk control. It caps how much damage a bad hour — or a bad version of you — can do.

Why limits are not pessimism: the variance

Many traders resist limits because they feel like planning to fail. The arithmetic says otherwise. Limits exist because losing streaks are normal, even for a method with a genuine edge.

Take a hypothetical method that wins half its trades. That is roughly where this plan's 1.5R target sits, and it is illustrative, not a claim about anyone's results. Pure chance then produces streaks like these:

Trades in the session Chance of at least three losses in a row
4 about 19%
6 about 31%
10 about 51%

And over a longer run of 200 trades at a coin-flip win rate, the longest losing streak is typically somewhere around six to eight trades.

Read that table slowly. If you take six trades a session, the consecutive-loss breaker will fire in roughly one session in three purely by chance, with nothing wrong with you or the method. The breaker is not an alarm that says "you have failed". It is a routine part of the method's operation, like a fuse.

The last sentence of that caption is the heart of this lesson. Look at what happened next on the chart and every instinct says the breaker cost money. On this morning, it did. But the rule is not about the market. It is about the person.

The fourth decision

Research on decision-making under pressure points one consistent way: judgement degrades with fatigue and with emotional arousal, and the person degrading rarely notices. Three consecutive stop-outs inside an hour is close to the perfect recipe for both. The trade you are tempted to take after three losses is not being chosen by the same trader who chose the first three. It is being chosen by someone who wants their money back.

That is why the breaker is set at three regardless of how good the next setup looks. The breaker does not exist because three losses prove anything statistically. They do not. It exists because the fourth decision after three losses is where traders reliably break their own rules.

COMMON MISTAKE

"One more, and then I'll stop." That sentence has ended more scalping accounts than any market move. If you hear yourself negotiating with a limit, the negotiation is the signal — the session is already over.

The trade cap and the clock

The trade cap and the session clock protect against the opposite failure: not tilt, but overtrading — taking more trades than the setup actually produces.

Overtrading doesn't feel like a malfunction. It feels like diligence. But every trade beyond your genuine setups is a lower-quality trade (we will call it a B-grade in Lesson 11), and every one of them pays the full toll. A swing trader who overtrades dilutes their edge. A scalper who overtrades pays a fixed, certain fee to dilute theirs.

The cap of six reflects what the plan normally produces. A typical London window offers somewhere between zero and five properly qualified setups. If you are regularly reaching six, the likeliest explanation is not an unusually generous market. It is a generous definition of the setup.

The clock matters for the same reason. Lesson 3 showed where the scalper's toll buys the most movement. After the window, liquidity fades, ranges narrow and the trend that powered the morning usually stalls.

The weekly limit and the wider view

The daily limit stops a bad session. The weekly limit stops a bad week — the kind where each session hits −3R and the trader keeps turning up the next morning assuming it will even out.

At −6R for the week, live trading stops until the weekly review. You may still practise on a simulator, but only the plan, and only as practice. The review asks whether the losses were valid trades meeting variance (it happens) or rule breaks, slippage creep or a change in market conditions. Lesson 11 shows how to run it.

One level further out, it is sensible to set a drawdown rule: if your account falls 10R below its highest point, you return to the simulator for a block of at least 50 trades before trading live again. That is not a punishment. It is a recalibration, done while the damage is still small.

The optional stop-win

There is one more limit worth considering, and it surprises people: a limit on good days. After an unusually strong session — say +4R — some traders simply stop.

The reasoning is psychological, not statistical. The euphoric brain and the tilted brain make strikingly similar decisions: bigger size, looser setups, fewer checks — only with more confidence. A trader who has just banked four wins in an hour is at real risk of taking a fifth trade they would normally grade B. The stop-win is optional, and you should test whether you need it by looking at your journal: what do your trades look like after a big morning?

Enforce it mechanically

Limits that live only in your head are suggestions. Make them physical.

  • Use your platform's daily loss lock-out if it has one, set to your daily limit in money.
  • Write the five numbers on a card beside your screen, next to your cost card from Lesson 2.
  • Keep a tally: one mark per trade, a circle for each loss. When you see three circles in a row, or six marks, or the clock reads 10:30, the decision has already been made.
  • When a limit fires, leave the room. Not to another chart, not to "just watch". Log the session, close the platform, and walk away.

Practice drill

Your journal shows five trades today: two winners, three losers, not consecutive, for a net −1.4R. No breaker has fired. It is 15:20 UK in the London–New York overlap, H1 bias long, and the M5 filter is passing.

Going deeper

Limits do not create edge. They truncate the left tail of your daily results, which protects your account and your psychology. They can also cut off some good trades, as the breaker chart shows. Over a long sample, a plan with limits may show slightly lower raw expectancy per day than the same plan without them, and much lower variance and drawdown. For a scalper, that trade is almost always worth making, because the real-world alternative is not "the same trades without limits". It is the same trades plus the ones a tilted trader adds.

Do not resize to make limits bite. Some traders, frustrated that their limit stops them early, raise their risk per trade "to make the trades count". This turns a 1.5% daily limit into a 3% one and changes nothing else. Risk per trade is set from the account; limits are set in R from that.

Slippage counts. Your realised results include slippage, so a −1.4R loss through a slipped stop counts as −1.4R towards the limit. If slippage is pushing you into the limit regularly, the problem is upstream — trading near news or in thin conditions — and belongs in your cost audit.

Count scratches honestly. A break-even exit at −0.2R or a time-stop exit at −0.3R is a loss for the consecutive-loss breaker. Calling it "not really a loss" so the streak resets is exactly the kind of negotiation the breaker exists to stop. If you want a different rule, change it at review time, in writing.

The limits are a test result in their own right. Track how often each limit fires. If the daily limit fires once a month, it is doing its job quietly. If it fires every week, something is wrong — with your costs, your window, your setup definition or your state — and the limit has just told you so cheaply.

THE RULES
  • Daily loss limit: −3R realised — no new trades once reached
  • Trade cap: six trades per session, whatever the results
  • Consecutive-loss breaker: three losses in a row ends the session; scratches count as losses
  • No new entries after the window closes (10:30 or 15:30 UK); open trades run to their bracket
  • Weekly loss limit: −6R — stop live trading until the weekly review
  • Limits change only at a scheduled review, in writing — never during a session

Summary

  • Five numbers govern every session: −3R daily limit, six-trade cap, three-loss breaker, the clock, and a −6R weekly limit.
  • Losing streaks are normal: at a coin-flip win rate, six-trade sessions contain three losses in a row roughly a third of the time.
  • The breaker exists because the fourth decision after three losses is where traders break their rules, not because the market is predictable.
  • The cap and the clock stop overtrading, which costs a scalper the full toll on every low-quality trade.
  • Enforce limits mechanically — platform lock-out, a card, a tally — and leave the room when one fires.

quiz.q: Your risk per trade is £40. What is your daily loss limit in money under the plan's default?
quiz.why: The daily limit is 3R. At £40 per R, that is £120.

quiz.q: Your session so far: win, loss, loss, time-stop exit at −0.3R. A valid setup appears. What does the plan say?
options: Take it — the time stop was not a real loss
Session over — that is three losses in a row, and scratches count
Take it at half size
Take it only if it has level confluence
quiz.why: The breaker counts any losing exit, including scratches and time stops. Three in a row ends the session.

quiz.q: At a hypothetical 50% win rate, roughly how often will a six-trade session contain three losses in a row purely by chance?
options: About 1 in 20
About 1 in 10
About 1 in 3
About 2 in 3
quiz.why: About 31% of six-trade sequences contain a run of three losses at a 50% win rate. The breaker is a routine event, not a sign of failure.

quiz.q: In the breaker chart, the trend ran strongly after the trader stopped. What does that tell you about the breaker?
options: It should be raised to five losses
Nothing on its own — the breaker is about the trader's next decision, not a forecast of the market
It only works in ranging markets
Breakers always cost money
quiz.why: The breaker protects against the degraded decision-making that follows a losing run. Some mornings it will cost a winner; that is its price.

quiz.q: It is 10:41 UK. You traded the London window and have taken four trades. A clean pullback setup appears on EUR/USD. What do you do?
options: Take it — you are under the trade cap
Take it only with level confluence
Nothing — no new entries after the window closes at 10:30
Take it on the 1-minute chart instead
quiz.why: The clock is one of the five limits. After 10:30 the plan opens no new trades, regardless of the cap.

quiz.q: In the USD/JPY drill, why was the trade allowed, and why did the session end after it?
options: It was allowed because the trader was losing; it ended because of the daily limit
It was allowed because all limits had room; it ended because it was the sixth trade
It was not allowed — five trades is the cap
It was allowed; the session continues until 15:30
quiz.why: Five trades, −1.4R and no three-loss run left room for one more. As the sixth trade, it used the cap, so the session ended there.

lessons.title: The Psychology of Rapid Decisions — and the Ten-Second Scalp Journal
lessons.summary: Budget your attention like risk, recognise your own tilt tells before they reach the order ticket, grade every trade A or B, keep a ten-second journal, and run a weekly review in R that audits the left tail first.
lessons.html:
Every lesson so far has assumed a trader who follows the rules. This one deals with the trader who actually turns up: tired some mornings, irritated on others, occasionally euphoric, and always fully convinced that today's exception is justified.

Scalping is harder on that trader than any other format. The trade cycle is minutes long, so a loss and the chance to "fix it" arrive almost together. Losses cluster, as Lesson 10 showed. Costs mean you can trade well and still finish a session down, which feels unfair. And the sheer number of decisions in a two-hour window wears down exactly the judgement the method depends on.

None of this is solved by willpower. It is solved by structure: fewer live decisions, pre-written defences, and a journal that tells you the truth when your memory will not. This lesson builds all three.

Attention is a budget

Every trading plan has a risk budget. Almost none has an attention budget, and for a scalper attention is the scarcer resource.

Decision quality is not a fixed trait. Sustained rapid choices under pressure wear down accuracy, patience and impulse control, and the person being worn down rarely notices at the time. A scalper making a handful of entry and exit decisions, plus a few hundred "is this my setup?" judgements in two hours, is doing one of the most mentally expensive jobs in retail trading.

The plan already spends this budget carefully, and now you can see why each piece is there:

  • The window is two and a half hours, not all day. Two focused hours beat four ragged ones.
  • The trade cap is six. Each trade spends attention whether it wins or loses.
  • Almost every choice is made in advance. Pair, session, size, stop rule, target, order types, news blackouts and limits are all decided while calm.

That last point is the deepest lever. Sort every decision in your process into two piles: those that can be made once, before the session, and those that genuinely must be made live. If you have followed this course, the live pile is startlingly small. Two questions, both binary:

  1. Is this my setup — yes or no?
  2. Is anything abnormal — the spread, the speed, the platform, or me — that says stand down?

Two yes-or-no questions is a load a human can sustain for a couple of hours. Twelve open-ended questions is not.

KEY POINT

Reduce live trading to two binary questions — "is this my setup?" and "is anything abnormal?" — and decide everything else before the session.

Rhythm and the ten-second reset

Watch a disciplined scalper and the striking thing isn't speed. It's rhythm. Candidate, check, act or pass, log, reset. The same loop at the same tempo whether the last trade won or lost.

Build that rhythm deliberately. After every trade, run the same ten-second reset: write the journal line (below), sit back, take one slow breath, and re-scan your pre-marked levels before looking for the next setup. It is the scalper's version of a tennis player's routine between points, and it does the same job: each point starts from neutral.

Add a break. Standing up and looking out of a window for five minutes every 45 minutes or so costs you a few candidate setups and buys back a noticeable amount of judgement. The market will produce another setup after your break. It always does.

The abnormality override

One instruction sits above the whole loop: stand down when anything is abnormal. The spread suddenly wide. Price behaving violently ahead of news you had missed. The platform lagging. Or you — angry, foggy, or checking your profit and loss every thirty seconds. Your method was tested under normal conditions; its statistics say nothing about abnormal ones.

Say it out loud if it helps: "Abnormal. Standing down." Then log the stand-down with a one-word reason, the same way you log trades.

Tilt: what it is and why scalping breeds it

Tilt is the state in which emotion — usually anger, or its politer cousin, urgency — takes over decision-making while leaving you fully convinced you are still being rational. Nobody on tilt feels on tilt. They feel decisive.

The classic sequence runs like this: a normal loss; a rushed re-entry; a proper loss; and then the moment the goal changes from executing the process to getting today's money back. That change of goal is the event to fear. Once today's result becomes the target, the checklist stops being consulted, size creeps up and stops become suggestions.

Know your tells

Tilt announces itself before it acts, if you know what to look for. The signs differ by person but fall into recognisable families.

  • Physical: jaw tight, leaning towards the screen, clicking between windows with nothing to check.
  • Behavioural: glancing at your profit and loss between candles; taking a trade within seconds of a stop-out; size quietly "rounding itself up"; the checklist being run in half a second.
  • Verbal: the voice in your head is remarkably reliable. It owes me one. This one's obvious, no need to check. I'll just make back the morning and stop. Any sentence containing "owes", "deserve" or "back" should set off the alarm.

Write your own list while calm — three physical tells, three behavioural, three phrases — and put it where you trade. You will not diagnose tilt from inside tilt; that is precisely what tilt prevents. But you can recognise a written tell the way you recognise your own name, even in a fog. Lesson 10's breaker and daily limit are the mechanical backstop for the moments when even the list fails.

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating tilt as something that happens to other, less disciplined traders. Tilt happens to everyone who trades fast enough for long enough. The professional difference is not that they never feel it; it is that they built a machine that keeps it away from the order ticket.

A-grade and B-grade: the overtrading audit

Overtrading is tilt's respectable-looking sibling. It feels like hard work: taking trades that are nearly the setup — a pullback that did not quite reach the band, a trigger that was nearly an engulfing, a level that was nearly marked. For a scalper it carries a double penalty. A B-grade trade has less edge or none, and it pays the full toll anyway.

The fix is a single letter in your journal, written at entry, before the outcome is known:

  • A — every item on the checklist passed.
  • B — anything less.

There is no such thing as a reduced-size B-grade trade. A B-grade trade does not get a smaller size. It gets no size. The point of the letter is to catch the ones that slip through anyway, so you can see what they cost.

Most traders who grade honestly for a few weeks discover the same uncomfortable and liberating fact: their A trades carry whatever edge they have, and their B trades are a fee paid to feel busy.

The ten-second scalp journal

Every rule in this course depends on data, and the data comes from one humble document. For a scalper the journal must be light — one line per trade, written during the ten-second reset — or it will not happen.

The working minimum, one line per trade:

Field Example Why it matters
Time 08:42 Results by half-hour (Lesson 3)
Pair and direction EUR/USD L Pair comparison
Grade A The overtrading audit
Tags Eng / 20 / L Trigger type, pullback depth, level confluence
Stop in pips 5.0 Checks the 5x rule and the maximum
Slippage +0.3 Intended versus filled price; your real cost
Exit T T target, S stop, BE, TS time stop, AB abnormality
Result in R after costs +1.3 The only unit you compare
State calm Calm, rushed, tired or tilted

Nine short fields, about ten seconds. No essays. Add a separate line for every stand-down, with the time and a one-word reason ("spread", "news", "me"). Over a month that column becomes its own education.

What the journal buys you is protection from the most persuasive storyteller in the room: your memory. Memory keeps the dramatic trades. The journal keeps all of them. Memory says the session went wrong because of one unlucky sweep; the journal says you took three B-grades after 10:00 while marked "tired".

The weekly review: thirty minutes, in R

Once a week, on a fixed day, spend thirty minutes with the journal. Review in R, not money and not pips, because R is the unit your process controls. Ask five questions, in this order.

  1. What did the left tail cost? In a rule-following scalping journal almost nothing should sit beyond about −1.5R. Every trade that does has a story — slippage through a stop in a fast market, or a broken rule — and each story gets investigated first, because a handful of −3R trades can erase a month of well-executed winners.
  2. What share of trades were A-grade? Then compare the R results of A and B trades separately.
  3. How do results split by half-hour and by state? Look for the hours, and the moods, that cost you.
  4. Is slippage stable, or creeping up? Creeping slippage usually means trading closer to news or later into thin hours.
  5. Is the sample big enough to conclude anything yet? Twenty trades is weather. Only hundreds are climate.

The monthly view asks bigger questions. Over a few hundred trades, is the plan's expectancy after costs actually positive? Has the market changed — spreads wider, your window quieter — in ways that alter the Lesson 2 arithmetic? Change rules only at review time, in writing, never mid-session. A rule you can edit while trading is not a rule.

Exit criteria, written in advance

Finally, write down — before you trade live — what would make you stop. For example: if after 100 live trades at minimum size my expectancy after costs is clearly below my simulator results, or the daily limit fires more than once a week, or my state column keeps saying "tilted", I pause live trading and return to the simulator or to a slower format.

That is not defeatism. Whether you are in the minority who can operate this format well is an empirical question. Exit criteria let the data answer it, rather than your mood on a bad Tuesday.

Going deeper

Euphoria is tilt with better manners. After an unusually good run, the brain makes similar decisions to the tilted one — bigger size, looser setups, fewer checks — with more confidence. If your journal shows B-grades clustering after big winning sessions, Lesson 10's optional stop-win is for you.

Sample size and the streak trap. At a hypothetical 50% win rate, ten-trade runs with seven or more losses happen about one time in six by chance. That is enough for most traders to start "fixing" a method that isn't broken. Judge the method on hundreds of A-grade trades; judge yourself on the A-grade percentage, which you control completely.

The state column is the most predictive field. Many traders who keep one find that "rushed" and "tired" trades are mostly B-grades. If that shows up in your data, the fix is not trading psychology. It is a shorter session, a break schedule, or not trading on days you mark as tired before the open.

Journal the stand-downs too. A stand-down log shows which abnormalities recur and when. It also gives you something to feel good about on days with no trades, which matters: a scalper who only feels productive when trading will find trades to take.

THE RULES
  • Two live questions only: is this my setup, and is anything abnormal? Everything else is decided before the session
  • Ten-second reset after every trade: journal line, sit back, one breath, re-scan levels
  • Grade every trade A or B at entry; B-grade trades get no size
  • Written tilt tells beside the screen; a negotiation with any rule ends the session
  • Journal every trade and every stand-down; review weekly in R, auditing the left tail first
  • Change rules only at a scheduled review, in writing; hold pre-written exit criteria

Summary

  • Attention is a budget: a short window, a trade cap and pre-made decisions leave only two live, binary questions.
  • Tilt feels like decisiveness; write your tells down while calm and rely on mechanical breakers when the list fails.
  • Grade every trade A or B at entry. B-grade trades pay the full toll for little or no edge.
  • A nine-field, ten-second journal is the only honest witness to your trading.
  • Review weekly in R: left tail first, then A-grade share, hours and states, slippage, and sample size.

quiz.q: Which two questions should remain as live decisions during a session?
options: Which pair, and what size?
Is this my setup, and is anything abnormal?
Where is the target, and should I move it?
How much am I up today, and should I keep going?
quiz.why: Pair, size, stops, targets and limits are all decided before the session. Only setup recognition and the abnormality check are genuinely live.

quiz.q: Which of these is the clearest sign of tilt?
options: Taking a valid A-grade trade after a loss
Standing down because the spread has widened
Thinking 'this one's obvious, no need to check' straight after a stop-out
Logging a stand-down
quiz.why: Skipping the checklist and phrases about the market 'owing' you are classic verbal tells. The other options are the process working.

quiz.q: In the A/B chart, what made the second trade a B-grade?
options: It lost
The pullback never reached the 20–50 EMA band
It was a short
It was taken in the overlap
quiz.why: The plan requires the pullback to touch or enter the value band. A two-candle dip well above the 20 EMA is not a qualifying pullback, whatever happens next.

quiz.q: A trader wants to take a B-grade setup 'at half size, just in case'. What does the plan say?
options: Fine — half size halves the risk
No — B-grade trades get no size at all
Fine, but only with level confluence
Only after an A-grade winner
quiz.why: A B-grade trade still pays the full toll for little or no edge. There is no discount ticket for a trade you should not take.

quiz.q: In your weekly review, what should you look at first?
options: Total profit in money
Win rate
The left tail — every trade worse than about −1.5R
The best trade of the week
quiz.why: Outsized losses are almost always rule breaks or slippage events, and a few of them can erase a month of good work. They are investigated first.

quiz.q: In the 'moved stop' chart, what did moving the stop do to the trade?
options: Improved it, because the stop survived longer
Turned a 1.5R plan into a 0.6R bet and a −2.7R loss
Nothing — the loss was the same
Made it a break-even trade
quiz.why: Widening the stop from 7 to about 18 pips cut the reward-to-risk to 0.6R and, when the new stop was hit, produced a loss more than twice the planned one.

lessons.title: Capstone — The Complete Scalping Playbook
lessons.summary: Run the whole method from the night before to the weekly review, follow three fully worked trades (including a valid loser) and a session where the correct number of trades was zero, and leave with the strategy passport and full pre-trade checklist.
lessons.html:
This is the whole course on a few pages. Everything from the previous eleven lessons appears here once, in the order you will use it, with nothing new added. If a step in this playbook surprises you, go back to its lesson before you take a simulated trade.

The playbook is built around one session — London (08:00–10:30 UK) or the London–New York overlap (13:00–15:30 UK) — on one pair. It has three phases: before the session, during it, and after it. Then come three complete worked trades, one of which loses, and a morning on which the plan's answer was simply "not today".

A reminder that matters more here than anywhere: every chart in this lesson is an illustrative training chart, not real market data, and every number in R is hypothetical. The plan is a method to test on a simulator, not a promise about results.

Phase 1 — Before the session (15 minutes)

  1. Check the calendar. Note every high-impact release in or near your window. Mark a blackout from 15 minutes before to 15 minutes after each one. If a major release sits in the middle of your window, consider not trading that day at all.
  2. Read your cards. Your cost card (all-in round-trip cost and the minimum stop it implies, from Lesson 2) and your limits card (−3R daily, six trades, three-loss breaker, the clock, −6R weekly, from Lesson 10).
  3. Set the H1 bias (Step 1). Long-only above a rising 50 EMA with higher highs and higher lows; short-only for the mirror image; otherwise no trading today. Check the nearest H1 level in the bias direction is at least twice your typical target away.
  4. Mark your micro levels. Prior-day high and low, Asian range high and low, the nearest 00 and 50 round numbers, the day's open. Five or six lines; no more (Lesson 8).
  5. Prepare the cockpit. M5 chart with the 20 and 50 EMAs, M1 chart beside it if you are running the M1 block, a one-click order panel with your size table to hand, a live spread readout, the journal open. Nothing else on screen (Lesson 7).
  6. State check. Tired, angry, distracted or ill? Write it in the journal and, if in doubt, do not trade. A skipped session costs nothing.

Phase 2 — During the session

Step 2: the M5 filter. For longs, the 20 EMA above the 50 EMA, both higher than six candles ago, at least 2 pips apart on EUR/USD, with a fresh swing high in the last 12 candles. Mirror for shorts. If the filter fails, wait.

Step 3: the pullback and trigger. At least two counter-trend candles, a low touching or entering the 20–50 EMA band, no close beyond the 50 EMA. Then one of three trigger candles: engulfing, rejection pin bar (wick at least twice the body, close in the outer third) or a close beyond the prior candle's extreme. If you are running the M1 block instead, the trigger is an M1 close beyond the last M1 lower high (Lesson 7).

Step 4: the exits. Stop 1 pip beyond the pullback extreme. Widen to your minimum if closer. If an obvious level lies within 2 pips beyond the stop, move the stop 1 pip beyond that level. Skip if the result exceeds your maximum (8 pips on EUR/USD). Target 1.5R from the fill. Room check: skip if a pre-marked level sits between entry and target.

The order. Stop-entry 0.2 pips beyond the trigger candle, cancelled after two M5 candles (three M1 candles). Bracket attached: stop-loss and limit target go in with the entry. Size from the stop, rounded down.

While the trade is live. Nothing — unless your block includes a tested time stop (close if not +0.5R after six M5 candles), a tested break-even rule, or an abnormality forces an emergency exit (Lesson 9).

After every trade. The ten-second reset: journal line, sit back, one breath, re-scan your levels. Check the tally against your limits.

The two live questions. Is this my setup? Is anything abnormal? Everything else was decided in Phase 1.

Phase 3 — After the session (5 minutes daily, 30 minutes weekly)

Close the platform when the clock, the cap or a limit says so. Check every journal line is complete, including stand-downs. Once a week, run the review from Lesson 11: left tail first, then A-grade share, results by half-hour and state, slippage, and sample size. Change rules only then, and only in writing.

KEY POINT

The playbook is three phases and two live questions. Every decision that can be made calmly is made before the session; the session itself is recognition and execution.

Worked trade 1 — EUR/USD, London, long: target

Before the session. Cost card: 1.0 pip all-in, so a 5-pip minimum stop. H1 bias long: price above a rising 50 EMA, higher highs and higher lows, the nearest H1 resistance about 30 pips away. Levels marked: Asian range roughly 1.0834 to 1.0842, the 1.0850 round number, the prior-day high at 1.0870. No high-impact news until 13:30.

The filter. At the trigger, the 20 EMA is about 6 pips above the 50, both higher than thirty minutes earlier, and the high at 1.0862 was made five candles before. Passes.

The pullback. Five counter-trend candles, a low at 1.0851 inside the band, no close below the 50 EMA. Qualifies, with level confluence — logged as "L".

The order. Buy-stop 0.2 pips above the engulfing high: 1.08548. Stop: 1 pip under the 1.0851 low is 1.0850 — on the round number, so it moves to 1.0849. That is 5.8 pips, inside the 5–8 band. Target: 1.5 × 5.8 = 8.7 pips, so 1.08635. Room: the prior-day high is 15 pips above the target. Size, with an illustrative £10,000 account at 0.5% risk: £50 ÷ (5.8 × £7.90) ≈ 1.09 lots, rounded down.

The result. Filled on the next candle, target reached about fifty minutes later. Journal: 08:52, EUR/USD L, A, Eng/20/L, 5.8, slip 0.0, T, +1.3R, calm.

Worked trade 2 — GBP/USD, overlap, short: a valid loss

Before the session. Cost card for GBP/USD: 1.4 pips all-in, so a 7-pip minimum stop. H1 bias short: lower highs and lower lows below a falling 50 EMA. No releases between 13:45 and 15:30.

The checks. Filter: the 20 EMA about 6 pips below the 50, both lower than six candles ago, a fresh low twenty minutes earlier. Pullback: four counter-trend candles, the high reaching the band, no close above the 50 EMA. Trigger: a pin bar with an upper wick about two and a half times its body, closing in the bottom third. All pass. Grade A, no level confluence.

The order. Sell-stop at 1.26560; stop widened to 1.26630 (7 pips); target 1.26455 (10.5 pips).

The result. Price dips to 1.26536, about a quarter of the way to target, then turns and rallies through the stop forty minutes after the fill. Journal: 14:12, GBP/USD S, A, Pin/20/–, 7.0, slip 0.0, S, −1.2R, calm.

What to change? Nothing. This is the trade from Lesson 5 again: a valid loss is the cost of finding out. If you find yourself writing "should have known" in the journal, check whether any rule was actually broken. Here none was.

Worked trade 3 — EUR/USD, M1 block, long: target

This trader is running a 100-trade block using the M1 refinement from Lesson 7. H1 bias long, the M5 filter passing, and the M5 pullback has reached the value band — the setup is armed, so the M1 chart opens.

The order. Buy-stop 0.2 pips above the shift candle: 1.09292. Stop 1.09236 (5.6 pips — no obvious level within 2 pips beyond it). Target 1.09376. Room: the M5 swing high this pullback came from sits above the target.

The result. Target. Journal: 09:31, EUR/USD L, A, M1shift/mid/–, 5.6, slip +0.2, T, +1.3R, calm. The 0.2-pip slippage goes in the slippage column; it is part of your real cost.

Session tally across the three illustrative trades: +1.3R, −1.2R, +1.3R. Notice how ordinary that looks. A method like this one makes or loses money in small, dull increments, and the journal is where you find out which.

The session with no trades

The most important session in this playbook is the one that never started.

That decision feels like nothing. It is the plan working perfectly. Here is what the morning looked like for anyone who opened the M5 chart anyway.

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating a no-trade session as wasted time and "finding something" to make it worthwhile. On days when the plan says stand down, the only way to lose is to trade. Log the stand-down and close the platform.

The strategy passport
Market EUR/USD first choice; GBP/USD or USD/JPY on raw-spread pricing. One pair per session. H1 for bias, M5 for the setup, M1 for optional entry refinement.
Wait for London (08:00–10:30 UK) or the overlap (13:00–15:30 UK). H1 bias from the 50 EMA and swing structure. M5 20 EMA above the 50 (below for shorts), both sloping, at least 2 pips apart, a fresh M5 swing in the last hour. A pullback into the 20–50 EMA band without a close beyond the 50, ideally at a pre-marked level.
Trigger An M5 engulfing, rejection pin bar or close beyond the prior candle's extreme. Stop-entry 0.2 pips beyond the trigger; cancel after two candles. (M1 block: a close beyond the last M1 lower high, cancel after three M1 candles.)
Stop 1 pip beyond the pullback extreme, moved beyond any obvious level within 2 pips. Minimum 5x your round-trip cost; maximum 8 pips on EUR/USD — outside that band, no trade.
Target Fixed 1.5R limit order, placed at entry, never moved. Optional tested time stop: close if not +0.5R after six M5 candles.
Avoid Asian hours on European pairs; 15 minutes either side of high-impact news; spreads above normal; flat or tangled EMAs; a target blocked by a pre-marked level; a third consecutive loss; the −3R daily limit; more than six trades; any B-grade trade.

Going deeper: from simulator to live

The method is designed to be tested before it is trusted. A sensible progression looks like this:

  1. Simulator, 200+ trades. Use replay to collect setups fast. Log every field. Do not judge anything until you pass 200.
  2. Read the results honestly. Expectancy after your real costs, in R. A-grade share. The left tail. Results by half-hour. If expectancy is not clearly positive after costs, the honest options are to fix costs (broker, pair, window), test one variation as a separate block, or stop. "Trading live to see if it's different" is not on the list.
  3. Live at minimum size, 100 trades. Real fills and real emotions change things. Compare live slippage and A-grade share with the simulator.
  4. Your exit criteria apply throughout. If live results sit clearly below the simulator over that block, or limits fire often, pause and return to the simulator. That is the system working, not failing.
  5. Scale slowly, if at all. Increase risk per trade in small steps, only after reviews, and never to recover losses.

And remember the course's first lesson. For many readers, the honest conclusion of this process will be that scalping does not suit their costs, schedule or temperament. Reaching that conclusion with a few hundred simulated trades and a clear journal is a success. You will have learnt cost arithmetic, execution discipline and self-review that make every slower format better.

THE RULES
  • One pair, one window, one setup; everything except "is this my setup?" and "is anything abnormal?" decided before the session
  • Bias on H1, filter and trigger on M5 (M1 only as a pre-chosen entry block); never trade against either timeframe
  • Stop beyond the pullback and beyond any nearby obvious level, inside your minimum–maximum band; target 1.5R; bracket at entry
  • Limits: −3R daily, six trades, three-loss breaker, the clock, −6R weekly — enforced mechanically
  • Journal every trade and stand-down; review weekly in R; change rules only at review, in writing
PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • Calendar checked; no high-impact release within 15 minutes of entry
  • Spread at or below my measured normal; platform responsive; my state is calm
  • Inside my window (08:00–10:30 or 13:00–15:30 UK); under six trades, above −3R, no three-loss run today
  • H1 bias set for this direction and still valid
  • M5 20 EMA and 50 EMA stacked in my direction, both sloping, at least 2 pips apart, fresh swing within 12 candles
  • Pullback of at least two candles reached the 20–50 EMA band with no close beyond the 50 EMA
  • Valid trigger closed: engulfing, rejection pin bar or close beyond the prior extreme (or the M1 shift, if this is an M1 block)
  • Stop 1 pip beyond the pullback extreme and beyond any obvious level within 2 pips; between my minimum (5x cost) and maximum
  • 1.5R target with no pre-marked level in the way
  • Size calculated from the stop and rounded down; stop-entry 0.2 pips beyond the trigger with the bracket attached
  • Grade written before entry: A only

Summary

  • The playbook has three phases — before, during and after the session — and only two live questions.
  • Worked trade 1 shows the full plan with level confluence and a sweep-zone stop adjustment; worked trade 3 shows the M1 block.
  • Worked trade 2 is a valid loss, and the correct response to it is to change nothing.
  • The no-trade session, decided at 07:45 from the H1 chart, is the plan working perfectly.
  • Test the method on 200+ simulated trades, then 100 at minimum size, with pre-written exit criteria throughout.

quiz.q: In Phase 1 the H1 chart shows price swinging either side of a flat 50 EMA with no clear swing sequence. What happens to the session?
options: Trade both directions on M5
Trade only the 1-minute chart
No trading today — Step 1 has given no bias
Trade at half size
quiz.why: The H1 bias is the first filter. Without one, the plan takes no trades, however tempting the M5 chart looks.

quiz.q: In worked trade 1, why was the stop placed at 1.0849 rather than 1.0850?
options: To make the position larger
Because 1 pip under the pullback low landed exactly on the 1.0850 round number, so the sweep-zone rule moved it beyond
Because the minimum stop is 6 pips
Because the prior-day high was nearby
quiz.why: Stops belong beyond obvious levels, not on them. The adjustment kept the stop at 5.8 pips, inside the maximum.

quiz.q: Worked trade 2 met every rule and lost. What should the journal and the plan record?
options: Grade B and tighten the rules
Grade A, −1.2R, and no rule changes
Remove GBP/USD from the plan
Require two triggers in future
quiz.why: It was a valid A-grade trade with a losing outcome. Changing rules after valid losses is optimising against noise.

quiz.q: Using the playbook's numbers, a long has a 6-pip stop on EUR/USD and the prior-day high is 7 pips above entry. What does the room check say?
options: Trade — the level is above entry
Skip — the 1.5R target is 9 pips away, beyond the level
Trade with a target at the level
Move the stop to 4 pips
quiz.why: 1.5 × 6 = 9 pips. A pre-marked level 7 pips away blocks the target, so the trade is skipped rather than reshaped.

quiz.q: Which of these belongs on the pre-trade checklist?
options: My last trade was a winner
The spread is at or below my measured normal
The trade feels strong
I am behind for the week
quiz.why: Spread is a live cost and liquidity check. Feelings and recent results are exactly what the checklist is designed to keep out.

quiz.q: After 200 simulated trades, expectancy after costs is slightly negative. What does the playbook suggest?
options: Go live anyway — markets differ from simulators
Double risk per trade
Fix costs, test one variation as a separate block, or stop — not trade live to see
Add two more setups
quiz.why: Live trading does not repair a method that fails after costs on a simulator. Change one thing and test it, or conclude the format does not fit.
